Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the prorogation proceedings. It is always a difficult matter to wind up the business of a session. As hon. members know prorogation is in the
nature of a ceremony and some careful preparation is required before matters can be finally arranged prior to prorogation. The other house has to conclude the business which may come over to it from this house, and the speech from the throne has to have its final printing. The deputy of the governor general will be acting for His Excellency in proroguing parliament, and it is desirable that due notice should be given to him as to the time to be present. These matters are all difficult to arrange unless the business of the house is concluded by' a definite time.
Hon. members will recall that early in the session I mentioned that if the house did not conclude its business by June 30 it would be necessary for the government to seek to have the session adjourned until September.
The Prime Minister did not really mean that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Oh, yes; I did. What I am about to say is that I am happy that that step has not been necessary. I should like to congratulate hon. members upon the way they have expedited the business of the house so as to make possible prorogation by June 30. I think splendid progress has been made and, as I say, I am pleased that matters have reached the point where it is not necessary to consider any adjournment of the present session.
I believe it is generally the wish of all hon. members that if possible, and without sacrificing anything in the public interest, we should wind up the business of the session today.
Two o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend says "two o'clock." That would suit me all right, but I want to make it clear that I should not wish to press the house unduly in the matter of time. I think by mutual arrangement it should be possible to have matters so planned as to permit prorogation at a reasonable hour in the course of the day.
What time has the Prime Minister in mind?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Most hon. members have left already for their homes. Tomorrow is July 1, and I know that several hon. members have obligations in their own constituencies which they assumed in the expectation that the house would be adjourned by June 30 at the latest.
Inquiries oj the Ministry

There is one other circumstance I should like to mention. The staffs of both houses of parliament, of the printing bureau and officials of the government generally have had considerable pressure put upon them during the last few weeks of parliament. As hon. members know, we have been sitting, not only in the afternoons and evenings but in the mornings, and on Saturdays as well. On behalf of the house I should like to express to the staffs that have had this extra duty put upon them our appreciation of the exceptionally efficient manner in which they have discharged their duties.
The house can best express its appreciation by making it perfectly apparent to the members of the staff that when July 1, Dominion day, comes, they may expect that the begin-nining of their summer vacation has been entered upon.
In seeking to arrange matters with a certain definiteness, if there are some questions which are of more importance to hon. members than others, and hon. members will let this side of the house know, we shall try to arrange to bring forward those matters immediately and leave the less contentious matters, if there are any that are still contentious, to the latter part of the proceedings.
That is all I have to say at the moment. It is intended to continue immediately with the estimates of the Minister of Finance. The next item to be taken up, as I was informed last night, is the important health program which has been announced in the house.
Mr. HOWARD C. GREEN (Vancouver South) : Mr. Speaker, I can assure the Prime Minister that the members of the official opposition will be only too glad to co-operate in bringing about prorogation today. We do not want to abandon our duty to give these estimates some consideration. We would be willing to sit right through without any recess for lunch. I should like to suggest one way of hastening the business of the house. For the last few days we have been working against a frog chorus, if I may use that expression without hurting anybody's feelings, from the government side of the house, sometimes led by one of the ministers, the refrain of which was "Carried, carried, carried." If the government members sitting behind the Prime Minister will allow the chairman to do the shouting of "carried," I am sure we shall get along much faster. After all, it is only human nature that opposition of this kind makes us all want to fight back a bit, and the result is delay; so, in the most kindly way, as the Minister of Labour would say, I suggest to

the members on the government side that they keep still today and let us get on with the business of the house.

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO INCREASE OF RATES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO INCREASE OF RATES
speechtext:
Mr. 'Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Labour?-although perhaps it is a question for the government as a whole. In view of the fact that the government is not proceeding this session with Bill 343, an act to amend the Government Annuities Act, against which there was opposition on the floor of the house, can the government say whether consideration is being given to restoring the rates on annuities to what they were prior to April 19?
Hon. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister
of Labour): I anticipated this question and have a short statement to make.
The Government Annuities Act was passed by parliament in 1908. Therefore it has been on the statute books for forty years. Its purpose was to encourage habits of thrift and provide a means whereby Canadian citizens could make reasonable provision for their security in advanced years through the purchase of annuities, a purpose which carried the endorsa-tion and support of every citizen of Canada. The act was intended to afford facilities whereby annuities could be purchased on the following financial basis: (a) that the purchaser would pay all the cost except administration; (b) that the government would pay the cost of administration. There is nothing
Inquiries oj the Ministry

in the act which provides any other basis. I would like to make it doubly plain that parliament in passing the act intended that the purchaser of the annuity would pay all the cost except the cost of administration.
Now let us examine how the cost is estimated. First there is the question of how many years an annuitant will require to be paid the amount started in the contract-in other words, how long will he live to draw the annuity?
Second there arises the rate of interest which shall be allowed on the premium payments made by the purchaser.
On the question of the interest rate, it is clear from a study of Hansard at the time the annuities act was introduced that it was originally intended that the interest rate should change with changing rates of interest prevailing in the bond market. In the original discussion on the bill, the Hon. W. S. Fielding, then Minister of Finance, stated:
The rate may be changed from time to time according to monetary conditions.
If it was the intention of the drafters of the bill that any specific rate of interest would be paid, such would have been provided for in the act. However, parliament authorized the government to fix the rate of interest by regulation. It is clear that this was done to permit interest rates to be readily changed from time to time to meet changing conditions. It was never the intention that there should be any substantial public subsidy to the purchasers of government annuities other than that provided by having the government pay the administrative expenses.
When the act was passed, the government had the responsibility of fixing the rate of interest. At that time government bonds were yielding 3-89 per cent and the government, in order to fix an even figure, rounded it off to four per cent. I have explained how the interest rate was fixed- and I will now attempt to cover the question of the other item entering into the cost, namely, how many years the annuity will be required to be paid depending on the expectation of life of the annuitant. In fixing the mortality table to be used, the advice of the best known actuaries in Canada was obtained and followed. Life expectancy, as will be appreciated, has lengthened since the act was passed. In fixing the rate which must be charged the purchaser, we have two factors to take into consideration, the life expectancy and the interest rate allowable. From these two factors, tables are prepared and it is on the basis of these tables that the contract rates are set. After twenty-

eight years of operation, it became evident in 1936 that there was reason to doubt the soundness of the rate tables because of increased life expectancy.
A senate committee investigated the matter and recommended a further study by Professor M. A. Mackenzie of the university of Toronto and as a result of his report, the rates were substantially increased on February 1, 1938. Not only that but he recommended the transfer of S8.941,195.84 in order to maintain a reserve in the fund because of the sale of annuities at less than cost prior to that date.
Now, what is the situation as at this date? We find that we are selling annuities at less than cost because life expectancy is greater today than it was in 1936. This is particularly important in view of the continuing trend toward longevity especially in view of the fact that many of the contracts will not become payable for ten. fifteen or twenty-five years from this date. Indeed some will not become payable until the year 2000.
In addition to selling annuities on the bargain counter because of the mortality trend, there is the fact that up to April 19, 1948, an interest rate of four per cent compounded yearly was allowed on money paid by the purchasers of annuities; whereas in the case of citizens who sacrificed to buy war bonds and Canada savings bonds, an interest rate of from 31 per cent to three per cent only was allowed. Such a substantial difference in interest rates is discriminatory and unfair as between different types of people who provide old age security in different ways. One group has been providing old age security by purchasing government annuities but a far larger group has been buying government bonds-victory loan bonds, war savings certificates, and Canada savings bonds.
At the present rate of sales and assuming money to be worth three per cent, if we continue to pay a four per cent interest rate, my actuaries have estimated that there will be a capital deficit of over $100 million incurred from the new business of the next ten years and this does not give any consideration to the fact that sales have been increasing very rapidly. Added to this capital deficit, had we continued on the mortality tables without consideration to the extension of life expectancy, there would have been a substantial additional deficit. Having regard for these facts, I am convinced this parliament would have found me very remiss had I not brought the matter to the attention of the government and recommended suitable adjustments. In arriving at the decisions made and put into

Inquiries oj the Ministry
effect by order in council, this government, has not departed one iota from the basic principles of the 1908 act.
I believe I have answered in my statement all the points raised by hon. members in the several debates on this subject.
Something has been said in regard to the fact that persons purchasing annuities after April 19, 1948 will pay more than those who purchased prior to that date. This, of course, is true, but it is not a new feature and is no different from the situation faced in 1938 when the last adjustment was made, nor is it any different from the situation existing in all kinds of insurance business. I maintain that the investment in government annuities is the best investment any one who is looking for security can make and I assert without fear of successful contradiction that the new rates are the lowest at which annuities can be purchased in Canada.

subtopic: STATUS OF ADJUSTMENTS INCLUDED IN SCHEDULE V OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: A resolution on the order paper dated December 5, dealing with the Geneva agreements, one of the matters for which the house was called together early last December, has been passed over. What is the position of the tariff adjustments that were included in schedule V of the general agreement? Parliament has not approved the resolution. No bill has been introduced. The announcement was made that this would go into effect. May the position be stated, so that the house may be clear on the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATUS OF ADJUSTMENTS INCLUDED IN SCHEDULE V OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: The tariff rates agreed upon in the Geneva agreements have been given provisional application in Canada and in other countries, as is contemplated in the agreements themselves. They have been given provisional application here by order in council. The statutory implementation of the agreements will take two forms. The resolutions, which still stand on the order paper, if adopted, will provide for the formal approval of the agreements entered into at Geneva. When that is done it will require legislative implementation by an amendment of the customs tariff. The resolution which stands in my name under government notices of motion is a formal resolution which must be passed, I am advised by my legal advisers as preceding a money bill. I am advised that an amendment to the customs tariff cannot be introduced unless preceded by a resolution. The amendments to the customs tariff will not be proposed until the resolution standing in the name of the Prime Minister, which is a general resolution asking for the approval of the agreements, has been adopted. In the meantime the tariff changes are in effect, and will continue in effect for the time being. The same position applies in the United Kingdom, and I understand the same position exists in t'he United States.

While we are on this question of price control I want to bring something to the attention of the committee which I think is important. I refer to the situation which has developed in our fellow commonwealth of Australia with respect to this question of price and rent control. I have had occasion in the past to refer to the constitutional position in Canada and the constitutional power of the dominion government to continue to impose price and rent control. I know that there has been the tendency in some quarters to consider that as a rather legalistic conception and one that does not have very much practical importance. The reason I want to say what I intend to say now is that the committee and the country may appreciate its practical importance; and I want to illustrate that point by outlining to the committee just what has happened in Australia.
As hon. members know, the federal government in Australia has been controlling prices and rent, over a number of years, under wartime constitutional powers which are not unlike those possessed by the federal government in Canada. Some months ago the Australian federal government-which is and has been for some years a socialist government-introduced a law into the commonwealth parliament to amend the commonwealth act, by adding to the constitutional powers of the federal government an additional power to be known as "XIVA". That power was to be inserted in section 51 of the constitution, which reads:
51. The parliament-
That is the Australian parliament.
-shall, subject to this constitution, have power to make laws for the peace,-order, and good government of the commonwealth with respect to:
Then there is a long enumeration of the powers, and the power to be inserted was: (XIVA) Rents and prices (including charges).
The situation in Australia is this. The federal government exercises such powers as are specifically given to it under the constitution, and those which are not mentioned there belong to the state. That is the reverse of 
our position here in Canada. Nevertheless the situation is analogous in this respect, that since "property and civil rights" is not in the hands of the federal government in Australia any more than it is here, they required this specific power. That law was submitted to a referendum-the government advocated its adoption, of course-and the government put out a pamphlet entitled, "The case for and against." This pamphlet may have been seen by some hon. members; it fully and fairly, I think, states the case for the adoption of the constitutional amendment, and against it. With the indulgence of the committee I should like to read the summary of the case "for". This is the heading: "Keep the protection you have", and it reads as follows:
A "yes" vote for commonwealth legislative power over rents and prices, will permit the continuance of-
Protection against inflation; fair rentals; security against eviction; real benefit from wage and salary increases; fair value for your money; protection of your savings and deferred pay; full value for your life insurance, superannuation and social service benefits.
A "no" vote will expose you to-
Inflation, boom and depression; profiteering, rack-renting and black marketing; eviction from your home; a scramble for houses and goods, with the rich always winning; decrease in the real value of your savings; industrial unrest.
Is that a fair presentation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That was the presentation of the case for the affirmative, a- vote for this amendment. And quite fairly the pamphlet presents the case for a "no" vote. It is elaborate but I will give the summary which is given in the pamphlet. It is headed "We urge you to vote 'no'." The reasons are given as follows:
We ought not to be devising ways and means of making wartime controls permanent; we ought to be reducing them as normal conditions are restored.
The ordinary citizen will get a better deal when powers of government are divided than when they are centred at Canberra.
After the bank nationalization experience, the Chifley government should not be given another blank cheque.
"Remote control" from Canberra has produced a vast and growing army of officials, a tangle of Ted tape, inefficiency, black marketing, and injustice.
In normal times, the controls in question can be far more effectively dealt with by the states, who have full power to deal with them, and whose administration would be much closer to the people and their needs.
Centralization of administration at Canberra weakens the authority of public opinion (as the banking business has shown), and produces a spirit of official tyranny which is a sinister enemy to true democracy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

The vote was overwhelmingly negative. I have the figures here. I shall not weary the committee with them; they are matters of public record. But as I say, the vote was overwhelmingly against the retention by the central government of these powers.
I am simply pointing that out to the committee for this reason. None of us can say with certainty how the Canadian people would vote if a similar issue were placed before them. In any case, that is not the procedure for making an amendment to the British North America Act. It would require an imperial statute. But it is significant that in Australia-where a labour government has been in power for some years and where presumably the idea of a controlled economy may have gained greater headway than it has here-the people in most decisive fashion declared that they did not wish to endow the federal parliament with jurisdiction over rents and prices.
Fortunately we in this country have followed what I consider to be the wise course of removing these federal controls in a gradual and orderly fashion. It has been a difficult procedure, particularly in these later stages. But I ask those who think we should have retained controls or should now re-establish them over a wide front to ponder well the results of the Australia referendum.
The Australian government now finds itself in this position. It has made no plan for the abandonment of these controls. The reports which I have received from the Australian information service indicate that the government there intend to toss rent controls back into the hands of the states about September 1. They have already abandoned rationing of beef, clothing, and the like, and they have abandoned subsidies on milk, textiles, yarn, raw cottons and so on.
Saskatchewan knows how to deal with the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should like to put this fact before the committee in as objective a fashion as I can, to reinforce the point which I have tried to make from the beginning in connection with this decontrol program: the federal government has not the constitutional power to continue these controls indefinitely. Parliament has given that right to the government until March 31 next. It is open to challenge at any time in the courts. One can appreciate the chaotic condition which might be created in this country if it were held, as it might well be held, that the federal government had no power to continue these controls indefinitely. I think that fact should be appreciated by every hon. member and by every person in this country. I have brought the Australian situation to the attention of the committee because I do not know whether its full implications have been realized in Canada.

But we have to judge the statement in the light of conditions. The minister says we have not the constitutional right to institute price controls. The referendum or Gallup poll taken in Canada some months ago indicated that 76 per cent of the people were in favour of controls. Of course if the government is not going to stabilize prices by government action of some sort the minister might as well tell the people of Canada there is nothing he can do to keep prices more in line with income. And if there is nothing he can do, then the people will have to take the necessary steps to try and keep their income in line with prices. So then where are we?

The discussion that has been going on about price control is exceedingly interesting to me. It is also a matter of vital importance to the Social Credit party, which believes it has the only possible solution to this price situation. Nevertheless I do not propose to follow my hon. friends in a discussion of the matter of prices, except to say

briefly that as far as I can judge the high prices we now endure had their fundamental and primary cause in the increase in the price of steel which was permitted back in 1946. That price increase has pyramided into increases in the prices of many commodities which are directly or indirectly dependent on steel.
What can be done at present to revert to the position we occupied at the beginning of 1946 would require some very wise men indeed to determine.
I will say, however, as all hon. members readily recognize, that there is only one sure way to keep down prices. That is to increase production. The big problem we must face, then, is how to increase production, and it is about that aspect of the matter I should like to talk for a short time, concentrating my attention on the beet sugar industry.
I am quite sure the people as a whole, and probably hon. members of this house, are not vividly aware of the degree to which the beet sugar industry could increase production in Canada. In beginning my talk I should like to point out that- on February 24 of this year I received a letter from a prominent beet sugar producer, in which he used these unhappy words: "We have been turned down on all counts." He was referring particularly to the response by the Minister of Finance to the representations of a group of men who approached him asking that certain adjustments should be made this year in respect to the beet sugar situation, which adjustments they believed would result in the signing of a great many more contracts for the production of beets this year all through Ontario and Alberta. The minister turned down those people, and for a few moments I should like to talk to the minister about that matter.
I might as well tell the committee what these men asked. They wanted the minister to agree to buy the sugar they would produce in Canada this year at the same price he would have to pay for Santo Domingo raw cane sugar brought to Canada, processed in Montreal and marketed here. They considered that a very fair and moderate request; but whatever his future intentions may be, the minister turned them down completely. They also asked that the fixed valuation of sugar for import should be reimposed. That was refused, too.
Some hon. members will recall that on May 13, 1948, as recorded at page 3911 of Hansard, I spoke on the subject of "Sugar beets and the Soil", a matter of vital importance to Canada at the present time. In the course of that speech I produced evidence to prove

that sugar beet culture always improves the soil. I should like to quote a short statement in that connection:
Statistics show an increase in the yield of crops in every country where the raising of sugar beets has been introduced.
That is taken /rom "The Sugar Beet in America," at page 257. It is to be found in reference 106, 1939, page 48, tariff board.
It is my purpose today to speak about "Sugar beets and Canada's Food Production", because these matters pertain directly to the question which we are discussing today and which is receiving the attention of the nation from coast to coast. The subject is timely. Everyone is talking and thinking about food. Hundreds of millions of people throughout the world are hungry and undernourished all the time, an experience which perhaps no one of us here has undergone unless it was during the war or some time like that. Scores of millions have not the soil resources from which to produce their required food. The average amount of arable and other cultivated land in all countries is 1-30 acres per capita, while in Canada it is 5-04 acres. Those figures were given in the Royal Bank of Canada monthly letter of June, 1948.
I should like to summarize an article which appeared in the Ottawa Evening Citizen of May 20 entitled, "The world's great need of food." This reads:
The world's food production must be increased to meet the needs of an additional 29,000,009 people each year, besides keeping pace with current needs, declared Australian director of agriculture Frank W. Bulock, in a review of the work of UjN., FAO.
He said a planned world agriculture called for the opening up of new lands, the application of every possible scientific aid and the prevention of unnecessary loss of cattle and crops.
That is exactly the text from which I propose to speak. If she is wise, Canada will recognize her duty toward the world with regard to food production and she will make broad her shoulders and assume an ample share of the food production burdens of mankind. We should not wait too long, because the need is immediate. People are hungry right now while we sit here in this chamber. They can see nothing but the prospects of being hungry for years to come. That is no small matter.
At the same time we should bear in mind those Canadians yet unborn who should have at their disposal soil as rich and as good as the soil which we possess at this time. If they are to have such soil we must adopt measures in this land that will preserve the fertility of 5849-390i
our soil to be passed on to future generations. What shall we do? Let us not forget the beet sugar industry in our planning.
By growing sugar beets our people can produce more food per acre-I want to point this out solemnly to the minister as a statement which he cannot gainsay-than they can by the use of any other crop known to man. So if we want to produce food in Canada let us not eoldshoulder the beet sugar industry. By using sugar beets our people can produce such abundance of food as only sugar beets can produce and actually improve their soil, as I have pointed out in previous speeches. From year to year they can improve the fertility, the fibre, the friability, the tilth and the health of their soil. They can increase everything that goes to make good soil.
May I say once more that this is a matter of importance, it is something for responsible men in a government like ours to consider. An acre of good Canadian land can produce food to the extent that I have indicated; and besides sugar beets are the surest crop there is in Canada, particularly in irrigated areas. Already there is beginning to be grave anxiety concerning the crops in western Canada. All over the land we are having drought which may result in almost complete crop failure. But there will be no failure in the irrigated areas where sugar beets are being raised.
An average acre of Canadian sugar beet land will produce ten tons of sugar beets. That in turn will produce 3,000 pounds of sugar at the average extraction rate of 300 pounds per ton. It will produce 2,000 pounds of dried beet tops at the average rate of 200 pounds per ton of beets. It will produce 1,000 pounds of dried beet pulp at the average rate of 100 pounds per ton of beets. It will produce 800 pounds of beet molasses at the average rate of four per cent of the beets, or 80 pounds per ton of beets.
But the production is much greater than that, as I should like to draw to the minister's attention. The 2,000 pounds of dried beet tops would be equivalent to 1,000 pounds of grain feed on the accepted basic formula that a pound of dried beet tops is equal to half a pound of grain. It would be equal to 1.500 pounds of alfalfa hay and 460 pounds of grain as used in a feed ration for cattle, this being worked out on the formula of 200 pounds of dried beet tops replacing 150 pounds of alfalfa and 46 pounds of grain.
The beet pulp would be the equivalent of 139-9 pounds of ground barley, 636 pounds of alfalfa hay and 44-2 pounds of molasses for every ton of siloed beet pulp. These figures are shown in the report of the Alberta beet growers for 1941, page 27.

We come now to the by-product, beet pulp. This valuable stock feed is used either moist in the condition it is in right after the sugar is extracted, or dried after the moisture has been processed away. Dried beet pulp is very valuable feed. There is no other product on the market which possesses its virtue. It is both an appetizer and a conditioner. It makes cattle eat more of other food, digest it better and improve themselves in condition. Milk cows fed with it produce more milk per pound of feed consumed. Feeders fed with it gain weight faster and more flesh per pound of feed. Show cattle 'take on a bloom which cannot be produced as economically in any other way. A ton of siloed pulp replaced 139-9 pounds of ground barley, 636 pounds of alfalfa hay and 44-2 pounds of molasses.
See Alberta Sugar Beet Growers, 1941 report at page 27.
What is the value of the by-product molasses? Beet molasses consists of sucrose, 50 per cent by weight, soluble salts and water. It is rich in potash; it contains some nitrogen. Beet molasses is useful as a stock feed and as a fertilizer. It is useful for yeast making and distilling. It mixes well with dried beet pulp. This has also been discussed in reference 106-39 at page 52.
Molasses is used increasingly in chemical processes, according to Messrs. F. 0. Licht in memoranda prepared for the economic committee of the league of nations, 1929, at page 25.

It is used in connection with yeast. Molasses was declared chemicals by munitions and supply during the war, as is recorded in the 1941 report at page 12.

A general idea of the value of beet byproducts in stock feeding may be gained from the following: experiments at agricultural college at Bozeman, Montana, found that to produce a 300 pound gain on each of twenty-one head of 650-pound yearling cattle required 67-2 tons -of wet pulp, 3-4 tons of beet molasses, 16-8 tons of cured dried tops, 8-4 tons of grain and 8-4 tons of alfalfa. That is referred to in the Alberta Co-operative Beet Growers 1938 report, page 10. Notice that every one of these ingredients used in feeding this stock, including the grain, comes directly either from the beets or from the rotation crops used in the production of beets.

There is no product in the Dominion of Canada that can produce milk to compare with beet pulp and beet tops. If we are to produce milk let us get the facilities with which our farmers can produce it. Mr. Chairman, I wish to refer to the question raised by the Minister of Finance before the hon. member who has just resumed his seat spoke, and that is the question of the constitutionality of price control. I presume most hon. members who belong to the legal profession, as I do, will agree with the minister's opinion on the question of the constitutionality of price control, but with great respect to those opinions, and with great respect to the minister, I disagree.
I am not competent at the moment to compare the Australian constitution with our own British North America Act and I shall base my opinion on the British North America Act alone. It is my opinion that this parliament has jurisdiction in respect of anything which by inherent nature is of national importance. I think my learned friends in this house will agree with me that this is the trend of the latest decisions of the privy council, and it is my opinion that the question of price control is a subject which by its inherent nature is of national importance. Therefore it would be competent for this parliament to legislate upon that subject. I simply rose to put my views on record with regard to this constitutional question of price control.

I note that such destructive criticism has come mostly from people who would not know the first thing about industrial management.
The sole purpose of many of those speeches -or I should say ravings-was to make out industry as a parasite, a leech feeding on the blood of its people.
To the gentlemen whose philosophy aims solely at establishing a socialist regime in this country, I ask this one question: "What has allowed Canada to develop into one of the most beautiful countries in the world, if not private enterprise?"
Hear, hear.

Why then seek to cast odium on people whose sole ambition is to produce for the benefit of their country?
And those great reformers, who take up more than half the time of the house, why don't they go to the root of the evil?
W orking men appeared before the committee. Were they questioned about things they knew? Were they asked why building costs are so high nowadays, when obviously such eosts absorb most of the liquid assets of potential owners? Were they asked why they only lay 350 bricks a day at wages ranging from $1.20 to $1.50 an hour, as compared to
1,000	to 1,500 bricks a day at only 60 cents an hour a few years ago?
No such questions were puit to them.
It might be told that no building tradesmen appeared before the committee, but I can reply that the example I have just given with respect to bricklayers applies to every field of activity.
If the practised critics we have in the house had had the courage to put such questions, they would have made themselves unpopular, and of course that is what we seek above all to avoid in this house. Some party members in this house have no more concern for the public weal than for the first pair of shoes they ever wore in their native land, beyond the seas.
Does a member believe he is true to his mandate when he adopts such a course of action? Does he believe he is doing a service to the working class, in representing its members as wretched people who are shamefully exploited?

I cannot consent to the decrease of $2,869,000 in this vote this year without offering a word of protest. I have been among the members of the house who have had words of praise for the work of the wartime prices and trade board since it was originally set up. In reply to the comments made by the minister this morning in connection with the referendum in Australia, I might say that if the people in Australia had had as happy an experience with their wartime prices and trade board as we have had with ours, the results of the referendum might have been different,
I think it would be extremely difficult to convince the majority of the people in Canada that to continue the wartime prices and trade board and subsidies for a longer period is not in the public interest. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre yesterday referred to an item that is of interest in homes where there are infants who cannot be brought up on human milk. He mentioned two cans of beef which were sold at the beginning of June for twenty-nine cents. The price of those two cans now is forty-two cents, an increase of forty-five per cent in this one item from June 1 until the end of June. I know that beef prices have gone up, but I would be surprised if the beef used in the manufacture of this product had been bought since the increase. If you had a wartime prices and trade board functioning as that board functioned during the war, enlisting the co-operation of consumers all across Canada, you would have some protection for the consumer, and you would not have a forty-five per cent increase in this one item in the month of June without action being taken.
The members of this group have spoken about possible action of the government following the report of the prices committee, but I am afraid that few in parliament or out of it will expect any vigorous action as a result of this report. I might remind the committee that two years ago, just in the closing days of the session, on going into supply, I had
the privilege of moving an amendment in connection with the milk subsidy. The motion was:
This house desires to record its opinion that consideration should be given to the continuance of the milk subsidy so as to ensure adequate return to milk producers and make possible the consumption of milk for the nutrition of the Canadian people without any further increase in the price thereof to the consumers.
Hon. members will recall that a majority of the members who were in parliament that day supported this amendment. The government promised to give consideration to the expression of opinion of the house, and consideration was given; but nothing was done to establish subsidies or to ensure that the consumers would be able to consume as much milk as before, without an increase in cost.
It is exceedingly difficult for the average consumer or producer in Canada to understand why the government can end the year with such a large surplus and- cannot find ways and means to provide subsidies for essential commodities. During one period in the war, more than a million of our youngest and strongest people were in our war services and war industries, and we were giving large quantities of food as mutual aid. But at that time we were able to consume more milk, 'butter and eggs in our homes than we did before the war, and more than we are consuming now. With so many of our veterans home, and with no disaster in most parts of Canada, with exception of British -Columbia, to interfere with our production, why it should be necessary to cut down our consumption of many of these foodstuffs ;s surely a matter -of concern to the Minister of Finance.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I must register my word of protest, I should like the minister to give the committee some information with regard- to the provision that has been made for historical documents to report on the work of the wartime prices and trade board, I might indicate that at some time we hope to form the government in Canada; and I am sure that the experience of the wartime prices and trade board during those years will be most useful. I have been disturbed a number of times when I have tried to get information from the wartime prices and trade board, to find that more consideration has not 'been given to preparing documentary information that should be available to all members of parliament. Though we do not all talk about profiteering as much as my hon. friends to the immediate left, and we do not ascribe the whole of the price increase in recent months to that cause, I think we are all as interested as they are in preventing profiteering and in prosecuting those who charge unjust and unreasonable prices. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The most recent and up to date information on that point is contained in the report of the prices committee, so hon. members have that. indicates that the staff of the board are constantly checking these matters when complaints are received. What I had in mind in connection with the procedure followed in bringing these matters before the courts really was this. Does the board, in making its investigations and laying these charges, do so in any sense as a deterrent, where they think there is simply reasonable ground for supposing a price is unjust and unreasonable, with a view to deterring others from charging similar prices? Or do they only prosecute in a bare minimum of cases, where they are certain there are unjust and unreasonable prices?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have discussed the general principles with the officials of the board. Let me say the board is not using these prosecutions as a form of terrorism. I told them prosecutions should be instituted only when they are satisfied that the evidence provides a good prima facie case. They need not have a case which, let us say, is beyond question; not many eases would fall into that category. It is the duty of the courts to determine whether a case is good or bad; but I think there is a duty on the board not to bring a man before the courts on a penal charge of this kind unless there is a good prima facie case. These provisions are not and should not be used as a means of persecution. Is that what my hon. friend had in mind?

Yes; and I entirely agree. Therefore it seems to me one would be justified in saying that, while the board is not too narrowly restricted in the cases it brings forward, that there has been only this comparatively small number of prosecutions under that provision is at least indicative of the fact, and certainly shows the board is satisfied, that the profiteering aspect has not had the effect on the increase in prices that is sometimes made out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is indicated in the report of the prices committee, which indicated that so-called profiteering was not a significant factor in the increase in prices.
The minister said there were some 7.000 investigations in May. Was that a typical month?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There were 7,300 odd in May, and I am told it was fairly typical.

I cannot understand why the minister should give a certain price for sugar to the cane producer in a United States dollar area and not be able to give a similar guarantee to the beet sugar producers so that their operations could be made secure.

May I tell the hon. member for Lethbridge that that is one of the fallacies of imperial trade. My hon. friend knows very well that the cost price of sugar in Havana is much less than it is in any British possession. It is the duties that make the difference in cost. Last year I asked a question in the house which was answered by the then parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, now the Minister of Fisheries. He told me that the price of sugar from British possessions was lower than the price of sugar from Havana, and that was true, not taking the duty into account. It is the duties on empire trade which make us pay much more for sugar. The British preference is a fallacy. I hope my hon. friend will understand that. I am all for the beet sugar industry, but I wonder whether beet sugar can sweeten things just as well as cane sugar does.
Just as well.
I do not know. I have been to some stores and bought beet sugar and I had to put great tablespoonfuls of it in my coffee to sweeten it.
The best chemist in the world cannot tell the difference between them.

It was not a chemist but my palate that told me. I found that its sweetening properties were just an illusion. Perhaps I am mistaken; I am not an expert like my hon. friend. But I want him to admit that imperial trade is a fallacy. The high duty on foreign sugar is imposed just so that we will pay less for sugar that comes from British possessions. Why should we buy our sugar from the British ministry of food? The
government there is making socialist experiments. Why should we buy our sugar from them? They control sugar, they control tea, they control everything, and afterwards they complain of poverty. We should deal, as we did before, with private merchants, and then Canada would be much better off. But as it is now we have to deal in a socialist manner with a socialist government. I am against it, and I trust I shall have the support of the hon. member for Lethbridge, who is so strong against socialism. This is the time to show his sincerity by protesting against the purchase of sugar from the British ministry of food.

Will the minister state the present position in respect to the exceptions in the domestic rental field control?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Everything is under control. The general rental ceiling is the ceiling which prevailed in November, 1941. New construction is in this position:	Houses built since
January 1, 1947 are completely free from control. That was announced some time ago. Other building construction is under control, but there may be varying ceilings, depending on the time of construction-in other words, buildings which were constructed between
November, 1941, and January 1, 1947. These new buildings had a rent established by the rental control administration as being the fair and reasonable rental for these premises, and that rent, when established, constituted the ceiling. Then there was the increase in rentals a year ago last May for landlords who were prepared to give a two-year lease. They were authorized to increase their rents by ten per cent.
As the committee is aware, there is a provision where in cases of exceptional hardship those who purchased their properties prior to January 1, 1947-I lam speaking from memory -may apply to the rental commissioners who have been set up 'through the country. If the commissioner is of the opinion that the landlord's need is greater, he can make an order giving the owner possession of the premises. That is a broad outline of the present position of rental controls.

With respect to that portion of it, besides the fixing of the rental itself there is the mobility of the tenant, shall we say. which is the point here under consideration. The wartime prices and trade board, with the help of the court, may decide whether or not the tenant may retain possession of a property or must move within the categories mentioned by the minister. The minister has made no statement recently with respect to the future of this domestic rental control matter. In the meantime many persons who have bought houses, hoping to enjoy possession of them themselves, are being denied that privilege by the wartime prices and trade board. In effect they are subsidizing the tenants without any assistance from the government, because the rental of the property which they bought and which they cannot have is fixed, and almost invariably they are paying rent in an uncontrolled situation or a higher rent. I think there is an element of subsidy there which the government is not meeting, but which the owner who purchased the property for occupancy himself is meeting.
I am in agreement with government policy to control rentals, but the government has not gone far enough in this field. The government has not alleviated the situation of those people who did not have shelter. Does the minister consider that the government, under the prices stabilization corporation or through some other agency, should meet the difference in rental of a bona fide purchaser who cannot get into his own house and the rental which he is receiving from his property? That has been going on for six months or so. He cannot get possession of his property. If he could
Supply-Finance

get possession of his property, perhaps we would not receive the number of letters that we do. This is a problem which to me is the responsibility of the minister to meet in some way. What does the minister propose to do about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This whole question of rental control has to be pretty carefully considered. It is one of the things to which I have been giving a great deal of thought, for reasons which I think the committee will appreciate. The dominion government cannot indefinitely continue in the field of rental and eviction control. One of the fundamental features of personal and property rights is that a man should be able to get into a house he owns if he wants to. It is an extremely difficult question. The prices committee has recommended that consideration be given to alleviating cases of hardship. That was done in certain cases by the setting up of these commissioners, and they have worked satisfactorily. I think it is possible that that may be somewhat extended, but certainly the dominion government could not consider going into the field of subsidizing individual owners of property because they cannot get into their houses to live in them. That would be an almost impossible task for any central government to assume. Possibly this is an appropriate place for me to make the few remarks I am about to make. Were the member for Peace River here I am sure he would once more register a strenuous objection to the fact that the estimates of the Department of Finance
always come before the house in the dying hours of the session. This has happened before and it is happening again. We do not feel that at this late hour we should engage in a prolonged debate on fundamental financial policies. On the other hand, we feel that it is a most important subject. We urge the minister to give consideration at the next session to bringing his estimates before the house at an earlier date, and we also serve notice that when that is done we shall be prepared to engage in an extensive debate on fundamental financial policies which we consider to be so extremely important especially at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

The reason the estimates are brought on towards the end, as a rule, though not always, is that opportunity for discussing financial policy occurs so frequently during the session. I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, that this matter has come up for consideration on the last day of the session when we are all in a hurry to get away. The increased grants brought in by the government are worthy of more discussion than they can receive in the last few hours of the session. The question of health is much more important than many of the other things we have been discussing

and on which we have had prolonged speeches. This is something that vitally affects the people of the country. I think every hon. member will agree that this matter should have been opened for discussion, and that it was worthy of a day or two in comparison with some of the other things we have discussed.
Censure the minister.

The minister promised full discussion on this matter when we should be discussing the items of the Department of National Health and Welfare. In view of the fact that the supplementary estimates were to be brought in, we agreed at that time that there should be full discussion, and even if this is the last afternoon of the session, I feel we should not hurry over this matter. Not only is it something which vitally affects the people of this country; it entails the spending of $30,000,000 a year. Even at this late date we should spend more time on this matter; if some of these other questions were worthy of consideration, this is even more important because it affects every member of parliament and all the people of this country.
In May the Prime Minister announced increased grants for national health. We welcomed the introduction of a plan that would help out national health. The Progressive Conservative party, realizing this need, has long urged a broader program for national health and for increased grants. During the time I have been a member of this house, we have repeatedly drawn the attention of the members of the house to the urgent necessity of action to overcome the deficiencies in our national health services. No later than March of this year I spoke on this matter in the house; I stated that the time had come to enunciate and put into effect a national health program for Canada. I further stated that the objective plan of this party was one which would bring health services to every Canadian citizen regardless of race, economic status or geographical position.
A year ago I drew the attention of the house to the necessity of a national stocktaking with regard to health. There is nothing new in the program that has been introduced. We welcome it and we welcome the increased grants. I believe that every member of this house, regardless of his political affiliation, approves any measure which will cut down mortality rates and relieve human suffering. Consideration of national health measures and anything that will better the condition of the people in regard to national health should be far above any political considerations.

Supply-Health and Welfare
In introducing this policy the Prime Minister stated, as reported at page 3935 of Hansard:
But what these expenditures may mean in the preservation of health, in the saving of human life, to say nothing of the lessening of human suffering and misery and not infrequently despair, is beyond calculation.
That is quite true. Mr. Chairman. But disease, death and suffering do not wait for a gradual extension of health services; nor 'have they waited until the government has taken action for the extension of health services. If this matter is so important now, it was important a week ago, a month ago, years ago. While life is within reach, it is cruelty to bar any opportunity to alleviate human suffering or reduce the danger of death.
Modern research is making tremendous progress in every major disease. Not only should we lend our efforts toward the elimination of disease and suffering, but in order to safeguard the state, we should make our people as healthy, physically and mentally, as we possibly can. There should be no geographic or economic boundaries in the opportunity for medical care. In the last hundred years we have made great progress and medical science has gradually brought disease under control. But it is unfortunate that the opportunity for treatment is not equal throughout the whole population. For that reason many people in Canada have not participated in the benefits medical science has provided over that period. In discussing this matter we must consider means by which these people may have the benefit of scientific advancement in the last century.
Today we have under consideration a limited plan; but while this plan is being discussed and put into operation, disease and suffering are still rampant throughout the country. That is going on at the very moment we are discussing these increased grants. Help is afforded by this legislation but during the time we are discussing it and during the time that will be required to bring it into effect, many preventable deaths will occur.
We are faced with two facts as far as health in Canada is concerned. These are facts which cannot be disputed, and I mentioned them at the time of the introduction of the estimates for national health and welfare. The first fact is that when our young men were called up for examination during the recent war some forty-two per cent were found unfit for service. If the proportion in that age group was as high as forty-two per cent at that time, the health conditions of other and older age groups must have been worse. The
other fact to which I direct attention is that the infant death rate in Canada is 5-02 per thousand live births, while the comparable figure in the United States is 3-8.
On these and other grounds I am going to criticize the legislation now before us. Surely further active measures are necessary to cut down our mortality rates, beyond the increased grants announced by the Prime Minister. It is admitted that hospital and treatment facilities in Canada are inadequate, and that is borne out by the very fact of these new grants. But there is another fact we should consider, though I am not going to speak at any length on this matter. In connection with the defence of our country we must remember that the picture has changed a great deal as far as warfare is concerned. Civilians are now in the front line. The atom bomb has been discovered, and we have heard stories of germicidal and bacteriological warfare. We must not blind ourselves to the fact that this is a highly important matter in reference to national defence, and I think consideration of national health matters should be joined with that of national defence. In the war of the future these two matters will be joined together, so that the health of our civilians has become of great importance.
The other important matter as far as national defence is concerned is this alarming proportion of unfitness in our young men. If we are to build a strong nation we must have healthy people. While maternal mortality rates, infant mortality rates and mortality rates from various diseases have fallen, there are still many problems that should receive our active attention. I am sorry that today, in discussing what is probably the most important matter as far as our people are concerned, we have only a bare quorum of the house. I am going to cite some of these problems, and then it will become apparent that these health grants only touch their fringe. We are discussing grants involving an expenditure of $30,000,000. That is a great deal of money; yet this is a short-sighted policy, because sickness is costing the people of Canada, in loss of time, loss of production and the cost of treatment, $1 billion a year. So we have a comparison between $30,000,000 spent on this important matter which costs the people of Canada $1 billion a year. In view of that estimated cost, surely this policy is short-sighted.
Much has been overlooked in bringing down these grants, and many matters of vital importance have not been considered. I spoke of the infantile mortality rate in Canada, so let us consider the record in that regard. One would have thought the loss of these young Canadian citizens would be a matter of primary importance, but I fail to see anything in
Supply-Health and Welfare

these grants or in any special grants to deal with this problem. In Canada we lose approximately 15,000 infants a year. In the last twenty years-and this is an amazing figure-that is from 1926 to 1945, we lost 345,000 babies. I believe every hon. member should fix that figure in his mind, so that next year, when we consider this question of national health and welfare, every hon. member will be aware of the great loss we have suffered in this way.
An analysis of these deaths shows that many of these young Canadian citizens could have been saved if they had been given an opportunity-and again I use that word "opportunity"-of adequate pre-natal and post-natal care. That is the answer. In previous speeches in this house I have stated the statistics of the various provinces with respect to the causes of death of these infants. The fact remains that we cannot afford to lose them, and we must do something about the matter.

There is also a grant for
tuberculosis and this meets with my entire approval. Tuberculosis ranks high as the cause of death in our nation, it being seventh in the list. Unfortunately it is a disease of early life and sixty per cent of deaths from tuberculosis occur in the most productive age group of from twenty to fifty years. Sixty per cent of all tuberculosis cases entering hospitals are in that age group.
Not only that, it is an expensive disease. There is something in the nature of a new cure for tuberculosis by the use of streptomycin. This is provided for patients in veterans hospitals, but the ordinary civilian must pay for treatment. I had a case some months ago, and I found that it would cost $250 to give the patient a chance to fight this disease. The cost to the taxpayers for assistance to the family of a tuberculosis patient is $2,800. The average cost in loss of wages and hospital care for a wage earner is estimated at S5.000. Those two amounts total $7,800, and this does not take into account the lost production while the patient is in the hospital.

Those figures clearly indicate that something has been accomplished in the fight against tuberculosis in the last twenty-five years. It is quite clear that more can be done. Given adequate grants, given help, we can fight this disease. We must remember that we are fighting one of the most expensive diseases that exist.
I come now to preventive medicine, especially as it concerns children. Sometimes we fail to recognize that many children die from

Supply-Health and Welfare
diseases which could be prevented. Annually we lose 1,000 children from preventable diseases, and no one can estimate the value of 1,000 children. The main diseases in this class are diphtheria, scarlet fever and whooping cough, and they could all be prevented if the proper inoculation was carried out. Much has been done by the provincial health departments working with their own resources to wipe out these diseases, and it will be only a question of time before they are brought fully under control, provided that we have adequate funds. The money being spent is small in comparison with that spent in connection with other diseases.
Apart from the contagious diseases, infantile paralysis still ranks high in the causes of death in spite of all efforts to counteract it. We have no answer to infantile paralysis; but we hope that in the future, given funds for research, given help, many of these children now in hospital may be saved from the crippling effects of this disease.
I come now to diseases affecting adults, and this is of particular interest to hon. members. We are all accustomed to reading in the papers of sudden deaths from coronary and cardio-vascular diseases, which simply means diseases of the heart and blood vessels. These stand high in the causes of death in this country. Comparatively young men, some of whom are making a great contribution to Canadian affairs, are suddenly wiped out by heart attacks. This is a matter that demands scientific investigation because we know little of the causes of these fatal attacks. It may be many years before we find this out and many unnecessary deaths may occur. More money should be spent to provide diagnostic clinics in a fight against these diseases.
I come now to psychiatry. Many people in Canada cannot afford to have psychiatric treatment, and even if they could afford it there are few high-class psychiatrists available. Mental diseases are on the increase. Apart from the mental hospitals in the various provinces, very little has been done to control and check the onrush of these mental diseases. Then we come up against the question of cost. The government has had some experience so far as hospitalization for these diseases is concerned. I shall refer to that later.
The cost of maintaining mental patients in our hospitals is simply enormous. It is interesting to note that in 1931 there were 31,686 patients in mental hospitals, but by 1945 the number had increased to 48,056. It must be noted that the population in our mental hospitals is growing at a faster rate than the general population of Canada. There is a
marked shortage of beds for mental cases, and this population would be much larger if the mental hospitals could take all who should be admitted for treatment. There is a shortage of 10,000 mental hospital beds in Canada today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We estimate 24,000.

I am sorry the figure is so much larger. The figure I had was 10,000. Everyone does not agree as to how urgent the necessity for treatment is; but if the minister says that 24,000 beds should be provided I accept that figure, because there is no dispute so far as the minister and I are concerned as to the necessity for more beds for mental patients.
Let us look at the expenditures in Canada for mental hospitals. In 1945 the total expenditure was $22,950,837. That is the last figure I have. In the matter of costs, to this might be added 14,000,000 man-days lost in production, or an equivalent of $50,000,000. I have mentioned that we had forty-two per cent of [DOT]our young men unfit, and, Mr. Chairman, of that forty-two per cent, at least one man in ten was rejected from psychiatric causes, and many medical discharges were for the same reason. Many estimates have been made of the number of Canadians who are ill of mental disease, and the cost in loss of production and maintenance would run into a staggering figure. The grant announced by the Prime Minister, while it is a help, does not begin to cover the problem. We can attack mental sickness as we have attacked physical sickness. We need a program of mental hygiene to cut down this terrific human waste. The place for early action is to deal with mental hygiene in children.
I have spoken in this house at different times regrading cancer, and there is no occasion to repeat those figures as we are all conversant with them. Cancer occupies second place in the causes of death. From 14,000 to 15,000 people in Canada die of cancer eacih year. There are two points I wish to make. First, thousands who would otherwise die of cancer are cured by early treatment. As many as
6,000	lives out of those 15,000 oould be saved for this country each year if given an opportunity of early diagnosis and treatment. The question of opportunity is the big thing so far as saving the lives of these people is concerned.
I am going to touch shortly on venereal diseases. There is a grant for that purpose in the minister's increased estimates. The provinces are concerned with the actual treatment, and many of them are doing excellent work in the treatment of venereal disease. It is a
Supply-Health and Welfare

hard problem to deal with. But the federal government should give leadership in planning control measures with the provinces and, aided by dominion grants, should co-operate with the provinces in their activities. That has been done, but the grant of 1500,000 yearly will not compare with the figures I shall give of the number of cases. These figures are startling, but I feel I should give them here. In 1946 the number of cases of syphilis reported in Canada was 15,217, and the same statistics show 26,286 cases of gonorrhea. Those are reported cases. It would be impossible to give the complete effect of those statistics, but it is sufficient to say that they add to invalidism and institutional care. Money could be saved here.
The other remark I wish to make before I leave the subject is this. I call the attention af the minister to the fact that pre-marital tests for venereal disease should be made compulsory.
Now a word regarding sickness in industry. There again the figures are astounding. It has been estimated that sickness costs the wage earners of Canada $135 million each year, and at the same time it costs the employers 8200 million each year. We must consider the health of our industrial workers from the point of view, not only of their own welfare but of the welfare of the state in sustaining production. Many industrial firms in Canada have health programs for their employees and have found the value of health services.
Nutrition-I am not referring to the fact, Mr. Chairman, that it is now twenty minutes past two and we have not had our lunch- must receive consideration if we are to better the physical condition of our children. In that forty-two per cent of our young men who were found unfit we must give consideration to nutrition, to which in the past we have given too little attention. We have not regarded it as important as some other things, but we cannot overcome this percentage of unfitness unless a program is designed to meet this problem.
I have cited conditions in Canada regarding tuberculosis, cancer, infantile mortality, preventable diseases, venereal diseases, industrial health, and nutrition. I could speak of many other diseases and maternal deaths, if time permitted. It is essential in the consideration of treatment that there be hospital facilities and a sufficient number of beds for treatment. The shortage of hospital accommodation has been a problem for years. We require 62.000 hospital beds for immediate use. To build
62,000	hospital beds at the present time would cost half a billion dollars to provide the proper accommodation. The building of new hospitals and the extension of existing hospitals is not

progressing in view of the high cost of construction. Many hospitals were constructed as municipal schemes and had to depend for their upkeep on philanthropic donations. We have all been through that. We must have some sort of scheme wherebj' the government can, by grants, assist in building new hospitals. The government is providing this assistance.
But not only are we short of hospital beds, we are also short of nurses. It is estimated that we require from 9,000 to 10,000 additional nurses in Canada to look after our population. This nursing shortage is a handicap on the hospitals in providing care for their patients. At the present time nurses are overworked and hospitals are short staffed. N'ot only is there a shortage of hospitals beds, but the cost of sickness and hospital attention has gone beyond the means of people in the lower income tax brackets. We had an example of that the other day. When the e<3timates of the Department of Veterans Affairs were before the committee a question was asked of the minister. He said that a veteran going into a hospital for non-pensionable disability, that is, for ordinary care, had to pay at the rate of $9 a day ward rate. That would be (he rate in the hospital, but care would have to be provided in addition to that. The government, which is in the hospital business, has found that the cost is $0 a day. What of the poor middle-bracket income tax man such as ourselves? How is he to pay this amount? How is he to pay when it is necessary for him to provide a private room for his wife and special nurses besides? I have seen these cases. I am aware of that, and the trouble which exists. Can one wonder that this is just a paltry donation in comparison with the great need that exists? It is something that touches every citizen in Canada,
There may be new methods of diagnosis and treatment. We are doing much about this in our hospitals, but the cost of hospital care has increased beyond the means of the average citizen. On former occasions I have warned the government of the dangerous situation which will exist if we were to face another influenza epidemic. I hope it does not occur, but the cycle is coming around again. Some time it will occur, and with a shortage of 62,000 beds and 10,000 nurses it cannot be anything but a national calamity. The Prime Minister has said that the proposed grants represent the first stages of the development of a national health program in Canada. Grants for the health survey and the general health grant will give some measure of assistance to the provinces. The grants for tuberculosis control are far below the requirements

Supply-Health and Welfare
when we consider the statistics that I have given today. All will agree that the grant for crippled children is an excellent, one. It is worthy of praise, but fthe amount of $500,000 divided among nine provinces on a per capita basis falls far short of the mark. The grant for cancer control cannot be criticized. Any donation that has been given to cut down the ravages of this terrible disease, a disease that cuts down one in eight of our population, is praiseworthy. One could not criticize a grant for that purpose. The grant for hospitals will help, but in view of the fact that we are short 60.000 beds, it is an urgent need. The cost of hospital construction has doubled. Pre-war, one would estimate that the cost of a hospital bed was about $5,000. That was the building cost. We can now calculate the amount at over $9,000.
