I know. Desperation has driven them to it; but I know of municipalities Which cannot afford to give half a million dollars. That applies to small municipalities. They have to depend on gifts for their hospitals; they have to depend on municipal grants. They simply cannot undertake it. The minister has only to go to the adjoining county, where they are considering the building of a hospital, to find that out. The same problem exists all over. Where are we to get the money? In the meantime, while we are discussing this question of grants, people are dying for the want of hospital care. It is something with which we must deal. We must be realistic about it and get busy at it.
In considering these grants we come back to our friend, arthritis, which was discussed in the house on a previous occasion. I am not
going to discuss it at length. I have talked arthritis here for three years. It is true that a small start has been made at Sunnybrook hospital; but in view of the fact that there are 600,000 sufferers, of whom 125,000 are totally incapacitated, it is only a paltry approach to a subject so vast.
In a week or so I shall resume my practice. Possibly I shall get an arthritis patient who will say to me, "Doctor, what is the new program? What are you going to do for me?" What can I say? I will say, "The Minister of National Health and Welfare is running a little affair up at Sunnybrook hospital. I have nothing to offer you. I have no new ideas. I have no new equipment. There is nothing further I can do." That is the position that every general practitioner in Ontario or in any other province will have to take. We have not received any help from this grant.
I might call the minister's attention to the fact, that the organization known as the Canadian rheumatic disease people-the name is something like that-diid not receive a grant from the government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No, but they are going to under this plan.

I return to some of the figures. We are spending $30,000,000 a year, but sickness is costing the people of this country $1 billion a year. You cannot estimate the value of human lives. We are losing these people. We lost 345,000 babies in twenty years. We are losing these people with cancer; we are losing these people with tuberculosis, and I could go on. I say again. Mr. Chairman, that this is a paltry approach to a subject so vast. But even at that, $30,000,000 will do a lot of good, and it will be a welcome addition to the relief of human suffering. But I still say, it is insufficient when one is dealing with a question which involves human suffering and human lives. They are not to be measured in terms of dollars and cents. When the Prime Minister introduced these estimates he stated:
But of all a nation's resources, its human resources are most precious.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has exhausted his time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Continue.

I am going to quote the Prime Minister's statement:
But of all a nation's resources, its human resources are most precious. The preservation in health and strength of its population is surely the best of all guarantees of a nation's power, of its progress and of its prosperity.
Supply-Health and Welfare

He said our greatest national asset was the health and well-being of our people. In view of the great need, and the statement of the Prime Minister, we have granted $30,000,000, but the Prime Minister still suggests that the health of the people is the greatest asset we have in this country.
Let me make this clear. So far as we on this side of the house are concerned, we have had this problem before us. We have been conversant with it. We endorsed the policy of national health in Winnipeg in 1942. We also endorsed the policy in 1927 when R. B. Bennett was chosen leader, and during the government of R. B. Bennett. I am attempting to show you, sir, that we are conversant with this matter. We have been alive to the situation.
In 1937 the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett introduced the Employment and Social Security Act. That act was very much the same as this and it did attempt to deal with the problem and did give increased grants, but nothing was done from that day on. The act went through the courts to the privy council and was declared ultra vires. Part of that act was later brought in by an amendment to the constitution, and I submit that something further could have been done at that time, when we got the amendment to the constitution, because I feel that the provinces would have agreed.
I have said before that the question of health services should be above any party politics and I believe that in this house it is. I am only sorry that we shall spend but an hour or so on it in the dying day of the session, when everyone is in a hurry to get home. It is not particularly because of my profession that I am interested in the subject, but I am aware of what is happening. I have had over thirty years' practical experience in this, and I did not get it from reading books. 1 am interested in the subject, and in view of that I think more time should have been spent, on these estimates. It is unfortunate that these estimates were not brought down earlier.
So far as our party is concerned, I wish to repeat and to make clear our position in this matter, and I will quote our policy. We are in favour of this, in co-operation with the provinces, and we will bring in a national health program. We will consider the question of nutrition and better health standards, and the question of research in the control of cancer, arthritis and other diseases, and we will provide assistance for the construction of hospitals and health and recreational centres.

There is no doubt about where this party stands on this legislation and this question of grants. We approve them and will vote for them, and we will vote for them even if we do consider the amount entirely inadequate to meet the great need.

If a layman may congratulate a professional man, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) on the excellent way in which he has presented his point of view and that of his party.
Before I go any further, I may say I will not take the length of time he did in going over some of the matters he has discussed before in this house. I will not repeat what I and other members of this group have said on previous occasions in support of a proper and thorough national health program.
May I get to the point at once and say, while we in this group welcome the announcement made by the Prime Minister so far as it goes, we are disappointed in the fact that it does not go far enough. In our opinion the least that the government should do would be to implement the promises it made to the provinces at dominion provincial conferences, with those provinces that have signed the tax agreements. There are some provinces, including the one from which I come, which have signed away their taxation rights in certain fields. So to speak, they have leased them to the dominion government, and yet the dominion government has not come across with its share of the bargain under the circumstances under which these agreements were signed. That is why I say this does not go far enough from the standpoint of the provinces which signed the agreements.
In Saskatchewan we tried to plan our health program along the lines laid down by the dominion government in its proposals to the provinces, so that if and when the federal government gets ready to fulfil its promises that plan will work in, without any undue or unnecessary upsetting of arrangements that have been made and the advancement that we have made.
I would impress upon the minister the necessity of giving favourable consideration to the making of special grants to those provinces which had the wisdom to foresee the importance of doing something before this plan was ever announced. They have made considerable expenditures and have made progress in that line; but now, as I understand, this is apt to discriminate against the provinces that have made headway in providing proper hospitalization and other care for their citizens.

Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is an important statement. May I assure my hon. friend that is not the case, nor will it be done.

I am glad to have the assurance, but until this moment I was at a loss to know how the minister would provide that extra help toward expenses that we in Saskatchewan have incurred during the past several years. I am more than pleased that I have taken the time of the committee if only to get that assurance from the minister, and if that is carried out I wish to thank him on behalf of the people of Saskatchewan. In the province of Saskatchewan-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: And the other provinces, all of which have done -wonderful work.

In the province of Saskatchewan during the past several years-I would say the past three years-we have approximately doubled our bed space in hospitals, with the help of those interested in supplying hospital accommodation in the various centres where hospitals had already been set up, and in the more remote areas of the province. The provincial government has helped the local authorities to establish hospital services for the people, with the result that, as I have said, we have practically doubled our bed space in Saskatchewan in the short period of two or three years.
As regards hospitals, while I do not wish to be critical of other provinces, I believe that in Saskatchewan, working along the lines of the proposals submitted to dominion-provincial conferences, we have laid the foundation, the groundwork, so that we can work in with an over-all national health plan. We have instituted in Saskatchewan complete hospital services for the residents of that province.
I have here a card that entitles me to admittance into a hospital on the recommendation of my physician or of any recognized physician in the province of Saskatchewan. If he prescribes hospital care for me I can go into any hospital in that province for proper treatment. I may add that if in the opinion of the doctor, or of any specialists whom he may consult, it is necessary for me to go outside the province of Saskatchewan, this card will enable me to do so. The card cost me a total of $5-
For the year.

Five dollars for the year, the maximum being $30 for a family, regardless of the number. Whether eight, ten or twelve members, the maximum is $30 in any case. That is something we have done in Saskatchewan to give the residents of that
province an opportunity to be properly taken care of whenever their physicians recommend hospital treatment for them. In doing that we found it necessary to provide that extra hospital space to which I have referred.
May I say with all frankness there are some people who will rise to their feet in this house and say they want to have a national health program, but who in their own provinces have failed to go as far as we have gone in the province of Saskatchewan. While that is their own business, what I object to is the procedure when they' or their friends go into the province of Saskatchewan, try to put as many stumbling blocks as they possibly can in our way in carrying out this plan in a proper manner, and endeavour to belittle it.
I say no province in the Dominion of Canada has made as much headway under as many adverse criticisms as has Saskatchewan in this connection. We are far from being satisfied yet, because we still think we have a long way to go. But we would have been able to go farther if the dominion government had lived up to the agreement as it was originally proposed, at least with those of us who signed the tax agreements.
In addition to that, I may say that every old age pensioner in Saskatchewan, whenever his or her doctor recommends hospital care, not only gets hospital care, but gets doctor's care and any other attention which he or she may need in that line. Old age pensioners, blind pensioners, plus those on mothers' allowance and their dependents are given complete health services free in the province of Saskatchewan.
In addition to that, we have free treatment for cancer. In that connection I should like to say that for quite a number of years in the past, even under the previous administration, some attempt was made to give special attention to cancer cases, and considerable progress was made. The present government went a step further and made the necessary provision whereby all cancer cases are treated free.
Just a few weeks ago at the city of Regina, a ceremony was held at the opening of a wing of the Grey Nuns hospital in that city, the construction of which had been made possible by the co-operation of the provincial government and with the understanding that part of the wing is to be entirely devoted for a number of years to cancer treatment and work. The former minister of health, who is now lieutenant governor of Saskatchewan, along with the present minister of health, and premier of the province, and members of the various political parties were present at the opening of that hospital which was a forward step by people who had sunk their party differences and rejoiced that they were able to make that
Supply-Health and Welfare

advancement with regard to the cause of health. Just from memory I would recall the words that the Premier of Saskatchewan used. He said that through hard work and sacrifices we had all realized the ambition for which we were working in the cause of health. I would commend those words to those who are prone to rise in the house and ask for an overall national health program. In fact, I would say, let them in some of these respects follow the example set by the province of Saskatchewan.
In my final word, may I appeal to the minister that as soon as possible-and the sooner 'the better-we get into a proper working arrangement with the provinces that have signed these agreements. If that is done I can assure him that the health program in those provinces will go on at a speed with which he will be well satisfied.

I wish to add a brief word to what my colleague has already said. I think one thing the members of this house agree upon is that, while in principle we are certainly in support of the sum being voted, it is totally inadequate when compared with the field that is mentioned as national health. This sum of $30,000,000 in a field of that size is, of course, quite inadequate.
I wish to refer directly to figures which appear in the proposals of the government of Canada to the provinces, in August, 1945. For example, under the heading of "initial benefits under health insurance," the total quoted is, roughly speaking, $70,000,000. If you add to that for other benefits under health insurance the figure of $78,000,000, you have already $148 million, which is the share of the dominion government alone. Then $13,000,000 more must be added under planning, organization and health grants, which together with another $13,000,000 estimated hospital assistance, would work out to about $175 million. In other words, roughly speaking. $175 million was proposed as the share of the dominion government to the provinces in the event that they entered into the tax agreements which were mentioned a while ago. The sum of $30,000,000 works out to roughly 18 per cent of that amount. In other words, the present proposal is about 18 per cent effective, having regard to the over-all picture, even so far as the federal government was prepared to go at that time. The minister may have other figures to quote which may alter that figure slightly, but I think I am fairly close to the mark.
I also wish to mention another inadequacy in the present appropriation and that is the conditions which are attached to it. For

example, we find in the statement of the Prime Minister on May 14 of this year the following proviso, as reported at page 3933 of Hansard:
In order to qualify for the grants, the provinces will of course be required to maintain at least their present level of expenditures in this field. This same safeguard will he attached to all the other grants it is proposed to make.
And farther on in the statement the same proviso is made in connection with hospital assistance, in these words as reported at page 3934 of Hansard.
One condition' which it is proposed to attach to hospital construction grants is that the province shall match the dominion contribution or better it, and that the dominion contribution shall not in any case exceed one-third of the total cost per bed in any project.
I think that proviso may have the effect of vitiating all the effectiveness there is in this provision in many respects, because in certain provinces in this dominion, in which assistance in this form is needed most, we may find they will get it least, because the provincial government in that case-and in some cases where the municipalities enter into it-may not be able to match dollar for dollar as the present proviso would ask them to do. We also find that in some provinces, and I mention in particular any one of the three prairie provinces, a complete crop failure in any one year, or a similar disaster, could prevent that province from carrying out its share of the plan. In that way they would lose the benefits to which otherwise they would be entitled. In view of the relatively small amount involved, I think the federal government should at least have made it a flat grant, regardless of what the province or municipality concerned is able to do financially.
I want also to commend the government on having provided assistance in the matter of mental health care. Some time ago there was on this subject a series of articles, which I think most hon. members read, in Liberty magazine. I have no doubt they were correct, since they have not been challenged by anyone; and conditions in our mental hospitals across Canada as described in those articles were deplorable. I am not proud of the fact that the mental hospital at Brandon, Manitoba, was given the doubtful distinction of being called the second worst in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The articles were not basically incorrect.

Only yesterday I received a twelve-page letter from one of the patients at the Brandon mental hospital. I am not going to quote him as an authority, of course,

Supply-Health and Welfare
nor will I repeat his extravagant language. Suffice it to say that he doubted the mental capacity of those who keep him confined there, and suggested that if the minister and his colleagues were to trade places with him and those confined with him, conditions in this country might be improved.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Sometimes I think he is right.

Another matter of which I am greatly in favour is the grant being made for assistance to crippled children. I regret, however, that it is confined to crippled children, because in most provinces of Canada- and I can speak of Manitoba in particular- with the exception of unorganized territory there is no assistance whatever from the provincial treasury for crippled adults. That matter is left entirely to the municipalities concerned, and some of our rural municipalities are not in a financial position which would permit them to look after these cases as they should be looked after. I understand that in Saskatchewan the provincial government now pays fifty per cent of the cost of such assistance to crippled persons, but in Manitoba and some other provinces the municipalities are burdened with the whole expenditure.
The last point I wish to mention is the fact that the proviso in connection with hospital grants in particular will work adversely in many rural areas of my province. I know many municipalities and towns in Manitoba have been trying to construct hospitals, and have expected financial assistance from this government. If the grant for that purpose is to be conditional upon an equal grant by the provincial government, and if the province does not see fit to come through with its share, I am afraid another great obstacle will be placed in the path of those municipalities.
In conclusion, I merely wish to add that, as far as I am concerned, I am happy to support this appropriation, but certainly I hope that the next time we speak about national health in this house we shall be able to talk in terms of a little more than $30,000,000 for the whole population of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
In a matter of such great importance, Mr. Chairman, as Minister of National Health and Welfare I think there are one or two things I should say at this time. I cannot cover everything that has been said in this debate, nor do I intend to attempt to do so, but I do want to outline a few points which I think are of great importance in relation to the program which is being discussed today for the first time.
This program is predicated, as properly and legally it must be, upon co-operation with the provinces. I am happy to say that about three weeks ago I called a conference of all the provincial departments of health, to which all governments sent representatives. I can only say that a spirit of the utmost co-operation prevailed with respect to relations between the federal and provincial governments represented at that conference in the matter of this health program. A second point I should like to make with respect to that meeting is that it was called before the moneys were appropriated for the national health program. I thought the house would sanction that move, so that we would be able to launch this program with a minimum of delay. I am now able to say that within the next three weeks we shall be having ex parte meetings. Next week I shall be meeting with two governments independently, and that procedure will be continued for the next ensuing period, so that this program may be put into operation as quickly as possible.
Let no one minimize the importance of this program; for whatever one may say, it is a program of the greatest significance. My remarks now are made in the knowledge that hon. members are prepared to deal with the steps to be taken by parliament to ease the burden of human suffering caused by disease, and all in this house act in this matter of national health in a spirit of non-political interest. Of that I have no doubt; but this program is so significant in its importance that I would be remiss in my duty if I did not tell the committee exactly what it means in terms of future commitments.
Under our constitution health is a matter for the provinces, and many provinces are very properly concerned about their jurisdictional rights in the matter. Anyone holding the post I hold must keep that concern constantly in mind. This program means that on the federal level, a level not responsible under the constitution for the health of the nation, from now on in one year we shall spend on national health more than we have spent in the past twenty-seven years. That is extremely significant. It means also that in a period of ten years we as a federal government will spend $300,000,000 to assist the provinces in the field of national health.
Let no one say that I think that is fully adequate, or that I am trying to justify what has not been done in the past. I am simply indicating the importance of this new health program. It is a far-reaching program, and perhaps its significance will be better appreciated when we compare our proposals with the federal grant system recently inaugurated
Supply-Health and Welfare

in the United States. As hon. members know, that country has the same constitutional relationship and problems that we have in Canada. The administration of health belongs to the individual states, just as in our country health is a matter for the provinces. The comparison I am about to make will clearly indicate, I think, the importance and consequences of the national health program announced by the Prime Minister. Both the United States and the Canadian programs contain many features in common; for example, grants for general public health services, grants for venereal disease and tuberculosis control, grants for cancer-, mental health and hospital construction. The United States grant for general public health services for the current fiscal year amounts to ten cents per capita on the basis of the 1947 population. The federal grant to our provinces under the program now before us commences at a rate of thirty-five cents per capita on the basis of the 1947 population and rises to a level of fifty cents per capita within a four-year period.
Mr. BURTON; Would the minister be able to say how- many tax fields the states have surrendered to the federal authority?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I am not discussing this on that basis at all; I am trying to outline the extent of our program. In the field of tuberculosis control the United States grant amounts to five cents per capita, based on the 1947 figures. The Canadian grant amounts to twenty-four cents per capita on the basis of the 1947 population and rises to thirty-two cents per capita as the program develops.
The figures with regard to mental health are even more impressive. The United States grants amount to two cents per capita on the basis of the 1947 population figures. The Canadian grant begins at thirty-two cents per capita on the basis of the 1947 population figures and rises to fifty-six cents per capita as the program develops.
The United States cancer grant amounts to two cents per capita on the basis of the 1947 population figures. The Canadian grant proposed in these estimates amounts to twenty-seven cents per capita on the basis of the 1947 population figures.
Finally, with regard to hospital construction, the United States annual appropriation amounts to fifty-two cents per capita, and the Canadian appropriation amounts to $1.04 per capita on the basis of the 1947 population figures.
Only with regard to the two smallest grants -namely, for venereal disease control and for crippled children-are the United States per capita allocations slightly higher than those
bMr. Martin.]
proposed in the government's program. The United States venereal disease control grant amounts to six cents per capita, and the grant proposed in this present program amounts to four cents per capita. The crippled children's grant in the United States amounts to five cents per capita, compared with four cents per capita in the Canadian program.
In total, the grants under the United States program for all purposes amount to eighty-two cents per capita of the population. Under the Canadian program the grants, taken altogether, are almost three times as great at the beginning, amounting to $2.32 per capita, and rise, over a period of years, to a maximum of $2.82 per capita of the population.
I mention these figures, because I feel that they will give in brief compass a clearer picture than might otherwise be possible of the comparative magnitude of this program taken in relation to what departmental undertakings in previous years have been, and also in relation to comparative undertakings by the federal government in the United States of America.
I cannot at the moment cover everything that has been mentioned today. I always listen with great interest to the speeches of the hon. member for Lanark because of their source, but I think he will be the first to admit that many of the matters which he discussed do not come directly within the sphere of federal jurisdiction. But with regard to the kind of spirit which he sought to impose on us, namely, that we should not have any limitation in our objectives, I fully agree. We cannot stop our work in trying to improve conditions that affect the health of the people of this country.
What we are doing about arthritis is not by any means, as the hon. member well knows, confined to Sunnybrook hospital. We are making arrangements with the provinces to give them particular health grants in order that there may be set up clinics throughout their jurisdictions on the basis of the Lord Horder treatment centres for arthritis and rheumatism in Great Britain.
At long last we have begun to do something in the field of arthritis, but it will take a relatively long time. These things cannot be done overnight. But finally we are doing something on a co-ordinated scale in an effort to bring about some improvement in this disease, which causes at least severe suffering to about 100,000 of our fellow citizens.
If the provinces are able to use their share of the $3,500,000 grant for cancer I do not think there is any reason why we should not have a complete system of free treatment for

Supply-Health and Welfare
cancer for those financially unable to pay for treatment in every province in this country. That is the objective about which there will be more said later after we have had further meetings with the provinces.
The program we are launching today is one of great importance to the people of Canada. We are approaching our role in a spirit of collaboration with those jurisdictions in our country that have direct legal responsibility in the field of health. It is only proper that I should say I have had from the provinces, all of them, the greatest co-operation in the inauguration of a program which I know the whole committee will agree means so much to our people.

I had not intended to say anything, but perhaps I might be permitted to say just a word at this time. I know every hon. member is glad to see something being done in this field. The minister made a comparison between the United States and Canada which reflects credit on Canada, but I think we should bear in mind that the states of the union have not surrendered their taxing powers to the central authority. I think that makes quite a difference in that regard.
There is another way to compare this $30,000,000 we are to spend. It is less than we spent in two days in 1944 on war. When one makes that comparison I think it indicates some justification for what I said when the Prime Minister came before the house with this program, that it was pitifully small. Then the minister said we are to spend as much this year as we spent in the previous twenty-seven years. I am glad to know that, but that does not reflect any credit upon the government which was in power during most of those twenty-seven years. We must bear in mind that in 1919 the program of the Liberal party, which was very attractive to many people, foreshadowed this health program, but it is only after twenty-nine years that some steps are taken to carry it out.
But I want to say that we are glad it is being done. I am glad to hear the minister say this will not involve discrimination against those provinces which have tried to build up high standards in this line. I am not singling out my own province, although it has gone farther than any other, but I would point out that the western provinces have gone a long way in promoting health programs for their people. It would be grossly unfair if, after having built up a high standard, they were told that, unless they could go farther and beyond that standard, or even maintain a standard which they had put into effect believing that agreements with the provinces with regard to health would be consummated, they would be penalized.
I am glad to know that something is to be done in connection with mental health. Many of us have read, during the last few years, articles dealing with conditions in our mental hospitals, and we know they are bad. The minister of health of my own province, who happens to be the premier, has taken a great interest in this particular disease, because it was in the field of mental hygiene that he obtained his Master of Arts degree some years ago. A great deal has been done there to segregate the various types of persons suffering from mental illness.
I am glad that something is being done with regard to arthritis, but there are other diseases in connection with which I should like to see the government make some grants. I am thinking particularly of sclerosis.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is covered.
That disease was hardly known a few years ago, but I have many personal friends who are suffering from it today.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We are taking a great interest in that.

I am glad to know
that from the minister. May I say, on behalf of the party which I have the honour to lead in this house, that anything the government does to promote the health and welfare of the Canadian people will be supported to the fullest possible extent. We shall be read}' to give all credit to the government that does it, whether it is ourselves or some other government.

I have a great interest in this matter, and I know that national health is of great interest to my constituents. My only criticism is that these grants are not larger. I support what has been said by those hon. members who have spoken previously, and I must say I enjoyed very much indeed the speech of the hon. member for Lanark. He never speaks on this subject without making a definite contribution to the knowledge of the members of this house.
I also support the criticisms offered by the hon. member for Dauphin, which I shall not repeat because of lack of time, but I think he made several pointed criticisms with regard to this plan.
I am going to support this vote, because I believe it is a real beginning in the development of a national health plan which the people of this country want. My corres-
Supply-Health and Welfare

pondence indicates that there are two subjects which are always treated on a nonpartisan basis by the rank and file in all political parties, and those are veterans affairs and national health problems. Great interest was taken in this plan when it was announced in the house by the Prime Minister, and from the correspondence I 'have I judge that the rank and file of all political parties are seeking the same objectives in this problem of national health.
Though the amount provided is less than I had hoped, I am glad that the government has made a start in this direction; and I am certain of this, that, because of the interest of the people of Canada in national health problems and because of the demand for a satisfactory solution of those problems, this is only the beginning of a rapid development in a national health program for this country. I believe that the minister has his heart and soul in this work, and I can assure him that he will without question have the support of the great majority of the Canadian people in what he undertakes in this direction.

speechtext:
I anticipated that there would be wide interest in this hospital construction program, because of the great number of questions put to me privately by various members and also by the correspondence which is coming in, and which I am at the moment simply unable to meet. Therefore, to inform hon. members about the problem and as to what steps should be taken, I propose to make a statement which I hope will be of assistance to them and to the country generally.
The purpose behind this hospital construction program is not to meet situations of the past, but to try to bring about a reduction in the existing hospital bed shortage in this country which, on the basis of Doctor Agnew's report, we estimate to be between
69,000	and 65,000. The program is not to provide relief as such to municipalities or to provincial governments. It is designed for one purpose, and that is to encourage the building of new hospital beds in Canada to take care of our growing needs and demands.
The hospital construction grant program is designed to remove the deficit in hospital accommodation that exists in Canada. At the same time, since adequate hospital facilities are a prime prerequisite for health insurance, and especially for hospital insurance, it will provide a sound basis for a health insurance program.
The grants will place emphasis on proper geographic distribution and proper allocation by type of hospital, thereby correcting to a considerable extent any maldistribution of hospital facilities. Further, by providing a more satisfactory distribution of these facilities, it is hoped that the program will contribute to better distribution of doctors and health personnel.
The demand for hospital accommodation has been rising steadily for many years. The factors which have contributed to this rise in the demand for hospital care include the trend toward obstetrical care in hospital, normal population growth, the great advance in coverage by hospital insurance plans, a greater appreciation of medical services including hospital treatment, and the financial ability of a larger sector of the population to pay for hospital services. While the demand for hospital care has been steadily growing, the increase in the supply of new facilities has been retarded. Since 1940 and 1941 the situation has become acute. During the earlier years of the war a shortage of materials and skilled labour stopped practically all hospital construction except that already under way. In the latter years of the war and the years immediately following, the tremendously increased costs of construction, plus the continued shortage of materials and labour proved discouraging to building committees.
The shortage of hospitals is particularly acute with respect to rural areas. I am saying this because the municipalities are becoming large cities, and I want them, to understand that we are going to deal with the provincial governments. That is the exact constitutional position. What we shall 'have in mind is a proper distribution of hospitals, not simply to give assistance because someone asks for it, but because, in accordance with plans jointly conceived by the provinces and ourselves, it is thought that a particular geographical section or area requires special treatment; consequently we intend to lay emphasis on the shortage of beds in rural areas.

On this general administration item I should like to refer briefly to the changes which were recently made in the categories of those employed in the House of Commons. The Secretary of State introduced a motion providing for a number of changes in the category of employment from temporary to permanent, and also, I believe, a separate order in council was issued providing for a number of appointments to those permanent positions. At that time I made an inquiry of His Honour the Speaker as to the number of employees of the House of Commons generally, and bow many were permanent, how many were temporary continuous and how many were temporary sessional; and of those, how many served overseas, how many served in Canada and how many saw no service in either war. Then I asked, with respect to the change from temporary to permanent category, the same questions: how many served overseas, how many served in Canada only and how many did mot serve in either war?
It is chiefly with respect to the employment of veterans and the granting of the veterans preference that I want to make some observations this afternoon. May I take one answer as typical. Question 6 was as follows:
Of the positions in the House of Commons staff whose category was changed from temporary to permanent employment by resolution approved by the house on May 3, how many are now filled by those who
(a)	saw service overseas?
(b)	saw service in Canada?
(c)	saw no service?
The answer was:
Of the 135 males on the temporary continuous staff shown in 2 (b), approximately 107 are occupying positions shown as permanent on the new establishment; of this 107, 43 served overseas; 5 served in Canada; 59 had no service in either war.
This means that forty-eight served in Canada or overseas and fifty-nine had no service in either war. Those are the new positions. That means that over half the appointments to the permanent positions are made from those who 5849-392J
had no war service. This is an extremely complicated matter, Mr. Chairman. I have been studying this reply to my question for some time, and I do not fully understand all the implications of temporary continuous and permanent employment. But it seems to me that the fact that less than half the appointments to permanent positions on the staff of the House of Commons are made from those with service in Canada or overseas in either war could give rise to some questions to His Honour the Speaker as to the extent to which the veterans preference is being followed in initial appointments to the staff of the house and in confirming those or changing them from temporary to permanent employment. First, I should like to say at least one word of commendation. I may have some complaints and requests later; but, despite the faults we may find, from the attention I have given these matters I feel that His Honour the Speaker and the Clerk deserve commendation for the efforts they have made, which as I understand it, have had two principal aims. On the one hand they have sought to move in the direction of a permanent establishment for the House of Commons employees. That is a far cry from the situation twenty or thirty years ago. I am glad that His Honour the Speaker during his term of office and Doctor Beauchesne, before he retires-if indeed that day is drawing near-should have played a part in having it laid down that House of Commons employees should have some permanency. I shall come back to this in a moment.
The other aim which I understand His Honour the Speaker and the Clerk have sought to achieve is that of keeping the House of Commons staff under the control of the House of Commons. I readily recognize, as has been brought out by the discussion we have had already, that this does create a problem, because we in the House of Commons do not want to see vitiated the principles laid down by parliament for the civil service commission. Yet I think there is something to be said for parliament being in charge of its own employees. If we did not retain that charge, the tendency would be for the House of Commons employees to become government employees. Already we have enough confusion along that line; already there are enough occasions when we ask the government certain things and are told to see His Honour the Speaker. Then, when we try to raise these questions in other ways, by presenting them to His Honour the Speaker, we are informed that these matters involve the expenditure of money and therefore recourse must be had to the government. I quoted that as a bit of digression, just to emphasize the desirability of maintaining control by the House of Commons over its own staff, without vitiating any other principles we have laid down. I am also satisfied that the employees of the House of Commons prefer to have it that way.
I offer that word of commendation to His Honour the Speaker and to Doctor Beauchesne sincerely and without qualification. However-and some hon. members may say, "Here comes the qualification"-I feel they have not gone far enough with the matter of the establishment itself. I may be told that one should be patient and wait for time to

When we have made our representations to the Minister of Finance, although he may show an interest in the matter, in the final analysis he delivers them to His Honour the Speaker. I do not expect his Honour the Speaker to work out a superannuation plan w'hen we have experts in the Department of Finance. But before you can have a superannuation plan for the House of Commons stenographers, you must have some permanency. I am prepared and the stenographers are prepared to accept some alteration in the plan that I have proposed.
I urge His Honour the Speaker to press this matter strongly. As I said a moment ago, it is only fair to the stenographers themselves. Surely this House of Commons should be a model employer. Surely we should not fall behind in the matter of old age security. I suggest that it is only fair to ourselves as well that this matter should be fixed up.
Before I sit down I should like to refer to another matter affecting House of Commons employees. This has to do with wage and salary increases. His Honour will recall that on March 24, before we went home for the Easter recess, he indicated that the internal economy commission was considering salary and wage increases, which would be reported immediately after Easter, all of which would be made retroactive to October 1. Later that same day, when questioned in the house, His Honour the Speaker said, as reported on page 2592 of Hansard:
The positions of all employees of the house are being considered at the present time by the internal economy commission of the house.
And later:
I have every reason to believe that all the employees will be perfectly satisfied.
As a result of that statement, all employees felt that increases would be forthcoming and would be retroactive to October 1. No distinction was made in that statement between

permanent and temporary employees. 'Rather than, make assertions myself on the basis of information that has been communicated to us, I would prefer Mr. Speaker to tell us the situation.
As I understand it, quite a number of employees have had increases granted to them, some by means of a vote of this house and others without the necessity of a vote. In some cases the increases were made retroactive to October 1. In the case of other employees, notably the men cleaners in this building, increases were granted but were made retroactive only to May. Similarly, I understand that the amanuenses who work with the Hansard reporters received increases, but again they were not made retroactive to October 1 as planned.
I have yet to learn whether the mechanics around the building have had any increases. The stenographers who have been asking for some permanency and for some pension plan have not had increases for a considerable time, and certainly have not had increases since the announcement was made by His Honour the Speaker on March 24.
I have tried to cover this matter in some detail, because we are all interested. I have tried not to speak in complaining tones or to be provocative. I think His Honour wall recognize the sincerity of the two points of commendation I made at the outset of my remarks. I feel that not only would the employees be happier, but all hon. members of this House of Commons would be happier if His Honour could give us some assurance on these two points: first, that there will be some kind of permanency and some kind of pension plan for employees like our stenographers and, second, that there will be wage increases or salary increases retroactive to October 1 for all our employees, as indicated by His Honour on March 24.

I should like to say a few words on this matter. I want to start by saying that I do not think His Honour the Speaker or the Clerk of the House has any more responsibility in connection with these estimates than the individual members of this house. The Clerk of the House is an employee of the House of Commons who works for us. The Speaker is an elected member who, because of his good judgment and ability, is permitted to sit up in the chair and be almost put to sleep at times with the speeches to which he must listen. He presides over the house; that is all. I do not think hon. members should take the attitude that those two gentlemen are responsible. I have never taken that attitude. Whatever is wrong with the

whole set-up in the House of Commons is the responsibility of every member of the House of Commons.
I look upon the staff of this house as working for the members of this house. We have heard many arguments in the house in favour of setting up collective bargaining machinery, national labour codes, and looking after everybody in the country outside the house, and then we take the attitude that the employees in the house are the responsibility of two people who have no more responsibilify in the matter than any one of us.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre went into this matter in some detail and I am not going to repeat anything that he has said. However I should like to deal with one branch, the stenographic branch. I think this offers a shining example of the way in which we are out of step with the times. Twenty years ago there were fifty-four stenographers in the pool, working in one room with one telephone and supervised by practically the same administrative staff that they have today when there are 155 stenographers, working in five rooms with six telephones. Incidentally, the rooms leave much to be desired. This indicates the terrific growth of the branch, but the administrative personnel has not increased at all.
The chief of the stenographic pool has had an increase of $400 a year in twenty-one years. That is certainly not keeping pace with the times. That is the only increase which has been given, despite the fact that there is three times as much work to do today. I think everyone will agree that a person who can manage a branch containing 155 stenographers and please the members of this house would need the patience of Job and the judgment of the Speaker. I realize the job he has on his hands and I think his salary is much too low. This matter should be looked into to see if something cannot be done.
This gentleman has one assistant who was recently appointed to that position. That person, too, is on the job all the time. That staff has the administration of the stenographic branch, which works for every department in this house. I think approximately thirty of the personnel work the year round. The three people I speak of, one a principal clerk, and the other two, the chief and his assistant, are on full time throughout the year. We all know what an assistant is. He is like a lance-corporal in the army. All the orders have to be carried out by him. He makes the unpopular decisions. He is running around in all directions. Recently the clerks of committees of this house had their salaries

increased. I find that the salary of the assistant to the chief of the stenographic branch is away below that of the clerks of committees.
The members of the house should not plead with the Speaker or blame the Speaker or request the Speaker or the Clerk of the House. I think we, the members, should say that we think the salaries should be brought into line with those of other employees of the House of Commons and with the salaries paid through the civil service commission. There should be no discrimination. That is our job. It is not our job to blame the two men who happen to be unfortunate enough to have to pilot these estimates through the house.
Then there is the question of a retiring allowance. There is a superannuation scheme for the civil service, and it is merely a matter of our determining whether the House of Commons employees should be brought under it or not. Every member of this House of Commons is aware of the fact that employees have been working in this building for twenty-five years who are still temporaries on small salaries, and many of them have about reached the retiring age. When they leave they have no pension, and no recognition is made of the services they have rendered to the members of the house during the many years they have been here. I cannot understand this business of a person working on a job for twenty-five years and still being considered a temporary. Any employee engaged in any capacity, no matter where, will have been able to demonstrate to his employer within a year whether he should be retained or not. If they have proved themselves worthy of being kept on, they should be made permanent, and whatever retiring allowance regulations apply in other departments should apply equally to them. I know a couple of old ladies who had worked in the stenographic pool for thirty years and who took sick and were laid off without half a day's salary and had to leave this building and get along as best they could without any income whatsoever. I do not think that is good enough for the members of the House of Commons, but the idea has grown up in the minds of the members that the Speaker and the Clerk are responsible. The members build a defence mechanism around themselves by blaming these conditions upon others. Actually the responsibility is on each and every member of this house, and not on the two persons we try to blame for not doing this or that or for doing the other.
The administrative staff of the stenographic pool is too small. I know that on paper there are eleven principal clerks who have been made
permanent this session, and the assumption is that they are at the disposal of the chief and assistant chief of the pool, but they are not. They work upstairs in somebody else's office and have nothing to do with the administration of the pool itself. So the administrative staff of the pool boils down to two or three people.
The stenographic pool is not merely a stenographic pool for the members of this house. They are cutting stencils for every department in this building. They are working for everybody, and they are on the job night and day just as long as the members of this house are working.
I am not going to tell the Speaker what kind of superannuation scheme should be worked out. All he has to do is to pick up a telephone and get in touch with the civil sendee commission, w'hich has experts who can work these things out. I believe that any employee of this house who has been working here for five years should now be made permanent, and the superannuation scheme should be made applicable to him. I do not think temporaries who are made permanents and come under the superannuation scheme should have to make up contributions for .the last fifteen or twenty years, which some of them otherwise would have to do. The government should make that contribution for them. I think five years would be far enough back to go. We, the members of this House of Commons, should determine here this afternoon that in future no employee who has been here for any length of time should be retired from the service of the members of the house and sent out on the street without some income such as is drawn by retired civil servants generally.
That is all I have to say on the matter, Mr. Speaker. I want you to understand that I am not blaming you or the Clerk of the House. I am blaming ourselves, the members of this house, and I am accepting my full share of the responsibility.

I am one of those who believe that the members of this house, to whatever party they may belong, are anxious to have efficient service from the employees of the house, and that they are also anxious to see that the nates of pay and conditions of work are the best that can be found in any part of the civil service of Canada.
While some suggestions and criticisms may be made in connection with the plan w'hich has been submitted this year, this, after all, is but the first real forward step which has been taken, and we cannot expect in the first year to find everything we might wish for. As a matter of fact, I have no doubt, that between now and the next session of parliament, the Speaker will have considered the suggestions

which have been made as a result of the publication a>nd approval of this plan, and that the lot of the employees of this house will be better for it. If one were to go through the different branches he could find any number of suggestions to make with regard to the employees of this house. Some have been champions of the stenographic staff, others of the messenger staff. I might, for example, say that the head of the maintenance and cleaning staff is probably not receiving anything like the salary he should have as the head of an important service, such as the cleaning and maintenance of this building. That is only a suggestion. I am sure that those who are responsible for establishing the salaries of the employees of this house will, between now and next session, consider -readjusting those salaries. I shall not take up time by going into particulars.
I should like to congratulate the staff on the floor of this house. I think the chief of pages, the assistant chief and all the page boys are to be congratulated upon the work they have done and the assistance they have given us during the session. I have one suggestion to make. These young boys have been working in the mornings lately, and I should like to see the Speaker consider giving them one or two weeks' salary, as we did last year, for the extra time they have to spend here at the end of the session.

I would not be rising to speak at this time if the Minister of Finance had assumed his proper responsibility last evening when I spoke on item 85 in support of the stenographers of the members of the House of Commons. I wish to draw attention to what I said last evening, because the Minister of Finance said he would turn the matter over to the Speaker. I do not think it is any concern of the Speaker. However, in a few words I am going to reiterate what I said last evening, to make doubly sure that the Speaker knows of this sad state of affairs.
My complaint is this. Until a year ago when these stenographers were given temporary positions between sessions in some of the departments of government they were classed as grade 2 maximum. For the first time last year they were classed as grade 2 minimum at a reduction of $23 a month in salary. That is unfair. I heard comments this afternoon on the splendid manner in which increases have come about, and all that sort of thing. Here is an instance of members' stenographers having their salaries reduced in the temporary positions which they are qualified to take when the house is not

in session. How can we expect to get good stenographers-and	we need first-el&ss
stenographers in this house-if that is the way they are to be treated? To the best of my knowledge, House of Commons stenographers have not received an increase in their basic wages for the past twelve years.

When His Honour the
Speaker is checking up on the different points which have been raised by hon. members who have preceded me, I wish he would check the cases of five or six members of the staff who were formerly on the protective staff. They are all veterans. Some of them were disabled. For one reason or another they were taken off the protective staff some six or seven years ago. Most of them are now messengers. One or two are on the cleaning staff. They were put on these other jobs but continued at the salaries they were receiving as protective officers. I understand that they have had no increases whatever. The salaries of other people about the building have been increased, but these men have not had any increase. They should have increases in the same way as the salaries of other members of the staff have been increased. I would ask His Honour to look into that particular situation.

There is one other matter that I should like to raise on this item. The debates reporting branch comes under His Honour the Speaker. That branch is known to hon. members as the Hansard office. It is a fine office. A wonderful spirit is shown there. It has always been a great help to the members of the house. This year two of the members of the staff are retiring, Mr. Frederic W. S. Galbraith, who is the associate editor, and Miss L. A. Kearns. I am sure that all hon. members will join with me, and will approve of my saying a word in praise of these two officials of the house.
Hear, hear.

They have been here for many years. Mr. Galbraith was a parliamentary reporter from 1912 to 1936. Since that time he has been the associate editor of debates. I believe Miss Kearns has been here even longer than Mr. Galbraith. They have always shown the utmost patience in their work. Sometimes I marvel that any individual could have such patience.
With our speeches.

Yes. They work late hours. They have a very difficult job. They have been very friendly and highly efficient. I am sure that we all wish them good luck in their well-earned retirement. They will not be with us another session.
It seems to me that these two officials of the house exemplify the ideal Canadian civil servant. I do not believe there is a finer civil service in the world than the Canadian civil service. As I have said, these two officials have shown the very finest spirit. We all wish them the very best of luck.

May I just add a word to what the hon. member for Vancouver South has said? I was going to say something in regard to the retirement of these two officials. I shall be brief, but I do want to associate myself, and the party which I lead in this house, with what has been said. From both Mr. Galbraith and Miss Kearns we have received every courtesy at all times. The efficiency of the debates office is proverbial among members. When you think of the state of the house at times, the interjections and all the rest of it, it is amazing that seldom has an hon. member to rise in his place and make a correction, so seldom that it is unusual to see anyone do such a thing.
Miss Kearns is in charge of the records and the indexing of the topics. After one has searched Hansard oneself to find a reference of years back one can go to that office and get the reference with great efficiency and great
speed. We all wish both Mr. Galbraith and Miss Kearns many years of leisure and of happiness in their retirement.
As the hon. member for Vancouver South has said, I believe these two officials, whom we are thus honouring today in these few remarks, are typical of the splendid type of person that we have generally in the civil service of Canada.

I am glad that the devoted services of these two officials, Mr. Galbraith and Miss Kearns, is being recognized here this afternoon. I want to join with all the others in expressing the appreciation of our group of the splendid service that we have been given. Sometimes I have wondered how it wias that some of the speeches that have been given in this house appeared so good when they came out in Hansard. I suppose it is because of the efficiency of the people in that office. At any rate I have found them at all times very helpful and very efficient, and certainly most devoted in their duties. We all wish them in their retirement long years of happiness.

As senior member on this side of the house I remember the time when Mr. Galbraith used to be a reporter, and he was doing that job just as well as he does the job of editor. I know Mr. Galbraith well, but I do not call on him every day I speak because I rely on him implicitly. I have given him a blank cheque to correct, but mot to add to my speeches. Sometimes I am dumbfounded to see what beautiful English is attributed to me, and it is due to Mr. Galbraith. When I want to know Where I can find a statement that interests me, or that I may need, when I want to know on what day I spoke on such and sudh >a matter, I have only to call on Miss Kearns. I believe she has the index at the tip of her fingers. She is always ready to help at any time of the evening we may call on her. I praise Miss Boyce very much also. She has retired. She also was most helpful.
I am sorry that Mr. Galbraith is going. I shall miss him. Sometimes at night, after a hard day's work, I used to go up to Hansard to have a little Chat with him and it was quite inspiring. It helped me to forget the vicissitudes of the day.
They are all great people. I have a great admiration also for Mr. Young. He _ is a former Hansard reporter and he did his job there very well, as he does as editor.
I congratulate them all on what they have done. I express my gratitude for the services they have rendered me, and I want them to know of my admiration for those services both to myself and to my colleagues.

Before I conclude I must say that we have a good service in all the departments. The stenographers have been mentioned. They are first class. There is my friend Cyril Wright, who was forgotten for a long time. He is most helpful. He looks after the mimeographed copies. He deserves something and I am sure he will get it. There are many others that I might mention. They are congenial and helpful. I might say the same about the constables, the same about the post office. The post office is a marvellous organization, when we think of the quantity of mail that passes through it, without a letter being put in the wrong drawer. The employees there are ready to serve, and some times when you have a letter to mail they will run back to get the last mail bag to make sure that it goes. They run as if it were a letter they were personally interested in.
I think the government has done well in all these respects. I congratulate Mr. Speaker and I congratulate the Clerk, the assistant clerk and the sergeant-at-arms. I wonder if it is due to their co-operation that we have now the best House of Commons service that I can recall. You, Mr. Chairman, and the vice-chairman must not forget that you have helped us a good deal at times. Without you life would be miserable.

I do not know that I entirely agree with the hon. member for Kootenay West. I know that there may appear to be discrepancies and I am aware that when you compare a man holding the position of manager of a restaurant with a doctor of philosophy in chemistry in some department there may seem to be a considerable discrepancy. I do not favour discrepancies, but I do not wish to see the salary of a parliamentary restaurant employee brought down; I want to see the others lifted up.
The hon. member mentioned this case by way of illustration. Somehow or other you find that sort of thing all through life and I do not know whether we shall ever get away from it. Take a parliamentary secretary, a stenographer. These people have to take a business course, and yet some slip of a girl may go into a factory as a rivetter and receive more because she is turning nuts in an assembly line. She will get more than a trained stenographer. The same thing is true generallj' in life and I do not know how we are going to adjust these things. Certainly a parliamentary stenographer is worth more than a girl dressed in overalls working in an assembly plant, but the same is true in life. A college graduate will go out and teach school for anywhere from $125 to $200 a month. Another fellow too lazy to get through high school drives a truck at $6, $7, $8 and $10 a day. As I say, these things happen in life and I do not know that the comparison is an altogether fair one.
I will say this, as far as the parliamentary restaurant is concerned, and I believe I express the view of many members. At least this year, and perhaps for the last couple of years, the parliamentary restaurant and cafeteria have done a much better job than they used to do. That is my own personal opinion. There might be need for a little further investigation of the over-all conditions as to salaries paid to the House of Commons help. I am not now raising one case and pitting it against another, but I believe there are discrepancies. I would urge those in authority to review them again. For instance, I understand that the protective staff who look after the senate door are paid a little more than those who look after the other door. I do not know why that is.

I may tell you that it was just a well for him, perhaps, that he did not run again, having regard to the black looks he got in some quarters. One could say plenty about what is going on around this house, and it is not said by members; but few have the courage to get up on their feet and say it. I particularly want to say that members on this side of the house, including myself, have been fighting continuously, but of course not openly in

the house; we think we can do more behind the scenes. I am putting this on record now so that the staff may understand that members on the Liberal side are thinking of the staff just as much as are members of the C.C.F. I want that made clear.

There is just one thing I want to say, before this item passes, with regard to what the hon. member for New Westminster has had to say. In my remarks I said that we were all responsible if there was anything wrong around this house, not merely the Speaker or the Clerk. Hon. members should not go to the Speaker or the Clerk and try to dump the responsibility on them. It is our job; and I hope that in future we will view it in that way.
The hon. member for Lanark asked whether the assistant chief and the principal clerk in the stenographic pool were veterans or otherwise. I wish to make my position clear on that point. I believe the veteran should get the preference wherever he is entitled to it, but there are hundreds of people in the employ of the government who served in that employment all during the war, and who were rejected for military service. near relatives of residents of Canada, the Canadian resident would undertake to make proper provision for the displaced person upon arrival.
Those who have come in to augment our labour forces have gone to the mining and forest industries, as well as to the clothing trade. Arrangements are always made so that these persons will have a job on arrival. The same thing is true, as the hon. member knows, of those who come to Canada to engage in domestic service. More requests are received for these people than there are persons to take positions. The lists are prepared and approved by the immigration branch and the Department of Labour.
I assume the hon. member knows that both these departments carefully screen the applications to make sure that a displaced person can be fitted into our community. I think the general impression throughout Canada is that the employment in domestic service of persons from these camps on the continent has been extraordinarily successful. I know a great many families where these persons have taken domestic service, and taking that as a fair cross-section I think I can say that this has been a very successful operation as well as being at the same time a humanitarian one. These persons have rendered real service in Canada.

I said a moment ago that we were ahead of any other country. I want to qualify that. I was going to make that remark myself. Canada has done pretty well in comparison with all other countries except Great Britain. 10,000,	the cost of transporting that number must account for a fair proportion of the money we have already appropriated.
Surely we have an obligation to the displaced persons in these camps who share the democratic viewpoints-and I use the plural- which we hold; and whatever we can do to relieve their sufferings I think we should do. I know that the number of persons in these camps has been reduced to some extent, but I hope that the definition of a displaced person will be extended beyond that adopted in
1946.	Some of those who today are fleeing from Czechoslovakia and other countries which have come under authoritarian or dictatorial rule, should have provision made for them.
But what I rose particularly to say was that there are many desirable people in these camps whom we are overlooking, and I have thought so from the time I was at the united nations meeting in the fall of 1946. I refer to the people of the Balkan countries, Lithuanians, Latvians, and Esthonians. They were at first rather frowned upon because their countries had passed under German domination, and by many they were viewed with suspicion. But many of these people are desirable, and in a higher educational category than those we have been in the habit of taking. I have learned from some of them that there is a disposition to frown upon the better educated groups in the displaced persons camps and bo bring those who might do the more menial tasks in Canada. I gave a clipping to the Minister of Labour the other day which had been sent to me by some friends in the country. It indicated that one of the girls who had just come across had said that she had to "act dumb" in order to get accepted. I do not know how true that is, but I had heard it before. I hope we shall consider this in all quarters of the house not so much as an immigration policy but as a humanitarian policy. Surely the determination of our democratic countries in the past has been that we should give refuge to persons who did not want to live under the regimes that had been established in many countries of Europe and from which they had fled. I like to think that Canada will follow that tradition and bring into this country men and women who will not return to their countries of origin because they believe in democracy and in freedom. anarchy. I do not wish to discredit the director of immigration and his assistants; they are able fellows.

['I know some would like to have it carried, but I have a few other things to say. A commission consisting mainly of doctors would not be in a position to understand the conduct of a legal investigation into a legal matter. Yet this commission consisting mainly of doctors retained no counsel to guide them! How in the world a group of five men could have considered themselves competent to inquire into so vexatious and so widely ramified a problem as that without a counsel to guide them, I cannot understand. Under the terms of their reference, and under the Public Inquiries Act, under which they were appointed, they had full power to select the finest legal counsel who could! be found in Canada and have him to guide them into the whole of their investigation; but apparently they considered themselves quite capable of doing this thing-a most astonishing situation!
Having laid before the house and the country the kind of thing that has apparently been attempted here, I shall not undertake to say what must have been the motive behind the men who set up that commission or planned it. I would not dare to suggest it, even. I would not suggest that the object of the whole thing was to discredit Mr. Kinchner. I would not like to suggest that the object of the whole thing was to whitewash the grievances of those unfortunate veterans, sixty-two of them, so that they would never again have any chance, even to be heard. I would not like to suggest that the object was to deceive parliament, although I must say that the kind of press reports that went out at the time the commission was first appointed to commence its hearings until the last, was certainly of the kind that would deceive the public, because the emphasis in all the press reports is placed on the question of whether or not there was anything wrong with the medical personnel in Shaughnessy hospital, a matter which had
never even been suggested by Mr. Kirchner, or by anybody else, so far as I know. The commission makes such a statement as this, for example. This was published in the veterans affairs publication in May, 1948, which all hon. members received:
McCann commission report that hospital facilities are satisfactory.
This appears under the signature of A. T. Paton, regional public relations officer, and reads as follows:
Medical and surgical treatment and the results obtained in Shaughnessy hospital are quite satisfactory and of a high calibre-as high as in any hospital in Canada. The percentage of successful operations performed there is, in our opinion, well in line with that obtained anywhere in the profession.
It was never even suggested that anything but such was true. Why should a headline in the veterans affairs paper indicate that the charge had been that there was anything wrong with the doctors in Shaughnessy hospital? Further down we have these words:
Their report stated, "The commission is satisfied with, and finds no basis for complaint concerning the organization, operation and facilities of Shaughnessy or the qualifications of departmental doctors. On the whole, the commission is fully satisfied with the high degree of competence of all departmental doctors."
If you were looking at these headlines, Mr. Chairman, you would find that because these later words are set out in black type this passage is the chief thing which the people were supposed to read.
I have produced sufficient evidence at this late hour of the session to give hon. members something to think about quite earnestly before we get back next year.
As a result of What I have feared from considering this whole affair, this McCann commission, has come as almost the crowning piece of evidence of evil in the whole Canadian pension set-up. I am not criticizing any one of the people in the pension commission, but something is entirely wrong, and this McCann commission is the strongest possible evidence that this house and this country can have, to prove that something is terribly wrong.
Considering all these facts, Mr. Chairman, I say the minister should take steps immediately to set up suich an organization as will enable the people of this country to satisfy themselves that the unfortunate veterans who happen to fall between stools, as these lads like Thom and Crowhurst and Harvey, shall have the right to ibe heard before some tribunal that shall be unbiased either politically or in any other way. How can our men have any confidence at all when they have to be tried before a tribunal with such a record as has been', 'Ways and Means', "indicated, and When they feel that they have to appear before an appeal board which is selected from the very men who ruled on their [DOT]cases in the first place? Where is the possibility of justice? I suggest to the minister that something must be done. I will not undertake to suggest what it ought to be, but something certainly must be done to gave our men something like a fair chance.
One more thing I should like to say, and it comes as a result of what I have read before, regarding Harvey and some of these boys. Apparently there is a demand on the part of somebody in the Canadian pension commission which has caused the doctors all down through the organization to threaten men who have been veterans, and who find themselves in such circumstances as have been described, with punishment if they write to their member of parliament. Have we got to the point where it must be conceded that in this country, when a man dons the king's uniform and risks his life for the welfare of the state, he thereby forfeits his title to his citizen's rights, that he no longer has the right to communicate with .his member of parliament, that he is in effect disfranchised, as it were? And must he be looked upon as an offender if he writes to his [DOT] member of parliament, and from that time forward be subject to all sorts of petty mean-mess and discrimination, even to the extent perhaps of being locked in a padded cell incommunicado? Have we got to that point? Some hon. members laugh. Well, the members who laugh would be simply appalled if I were to give evidence of a man who spoke to me three days ago, whose word would never be questioned, and who told me exactly what had been threatened him because he had asked for the milk which his doctor had prescribed in the hospital in which he was taken care of. That sort of thing must cease to be."]

There may be the occasional feed merchant who was fortunate enough to have some of the grain at the close on October 21 and who sold it afterwards.
